genres.name: Spirituals and gospel
genres.text: Spirituals emerged in the nineteenth century among enslaved African Americans in the southern United States; in the Black churches of the 1920s and 1930s they grew into gospel: religious songs in several voices, with call and response. From 1938 Sister Rosetta Tharpe recorded gospel songs with the rhythm and swing of jazz, and in the 1940s she was already playing solos on an electric guitar. Through singers who had learned to sing in church, gospel became one of the roots of soul.
genres.listen: Strange Things Happening Every Day is a gospel song, but if you ignore the words, you hear a driving piano and a guitar solo straight out of rhythm and blues.

tracks.title: Move On Up a Little Higher

genres.name: Delta blues
genres.text: The blues grew up around 1890 out of the work songs, hollers and spirituals of the Black rural population of the South, with the Mississippi Delta as a key region. Its hallmarks are the 12-bar form with AAB lyrics, blue notes and slide guitar. Robert Johnson recorded 29 songs in all, in 1936 and 1937.
genres.listen: Count the bars as you listen to Cross Road Blues: Johnson follows the words, stretching the form or moving on to the next chord early.

genres.name: Ragtime
genres.text: Ragtime was the first African American musical style to be sold on a large scale as sheet music. The left hand plays a march bass, the right hand syncopations against the beat, and the form is built from strains of sixteen bars. Scott Joplin's Maple Leaf Rag was published in 1899 in Sedalia, Missouri.
genres.listen: Listen to the contrast between the steady march bass in the left hand and the syncopations in the right.

genres.name: Appalachian folk (mountain music)
genres.text: From the eighteenth century onwards, immigrants from Scotland, England and Ireland brought ballads and dance music with them to the Appalachians. The fiddle played the jigs and reels of Scotland and Ireland; in the Appalachians these turned mostly into fast breakdowns in 2/4 time. Alongside the fiddle came the banjo, which is African American in origin. Songs passed by word of mouth from singer to singer: the folk process.
genres.listen: In the Irish Swallowtail Jig, one of the roots of this music, can you hear the two heavy beats in each bar, each of them divided into three?

mixtapes.heading: House of the Rising Sun: zes versies

genres.name: Classic blues
genres.text: In the 1920s the best-selling blues records were made by women. Classic blues is urban blues, sung by women from the theatre and the tent shows and backed by a band of piano, horns and sometimes a banjo. Bessie Smith, the Empress of the Blues, recorded Downhearted Blues in 1923.
genres.listen: Notice the AAB form of the lyrics, and how the singer, not the guitarist, is the centre of the recording.

mixtapes.heading: Bessie Smith, Empress of the Blues

genres.name: New Orleans jazz
genres.text: In New Orleans, around 1900, jazz grew out of the brass bands; later it was also called Dixieland or hot jazz. Cornet, clarinet and trombone improvise at the same time over banjo, tuba and drums: collective improvisation. The first jazz record appeared in 1917, made by the white Original Dixieland Jass Band.
genres.listen: Follow the division of roles: the cornet plays the melody, the clarinet weaves decorations above it and the trombone slides along underneath.

tracks.title: When the Saints Go Marching In

genres.name: Swing and big band
genres.text: In the 1930s the New Orleans band grew into the big band of twelve to seventeen musicians, with an arranger who wrote riffs for the sections. The eighth notes are played long-short and the bass walks on all four beats. Duke Ellington led the orchestra at the Cotton Club in Harlem; Benny Goodman, who was white, became the 'King of Swing'.
genres.listen: In Take the 'A' Train, can you hear the AABA form and the way the saxophones and the brass answer each other?

tracks.artist: Benny Goodman and His Orchestra met Charlie Christian
tracks.title: Solo Flight
I've Got You Under My Skin

genres.name: Tin Pan Alley
genres.text: From around 1885 music publishers set up shop close together in Manhattan, and from the 1890s mainly on West 28th Street. Songwriters wrote the songs, publishers sold them as sheet music and song pluggers demonstrated them; from the 1920s the 32-bar song in AABA form became the standard. Irving Berlin, George Gershwin and Cole Porter were the big names.
genres.listen: In White Christmas, hear how Bing Crosby sings softly and intimately, as if he were right beside you, thanks to the microphone: crooning.

mixtapes.heading: Van AABA naar couplet en refrein

genres.name: Country
genres.text: In the 1920s radio and the gramophone record turned mountain music into country. Ralph Peer's recordings in Bristol in 1927, with the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers, are seen as its starting point; the Grand Ole Opry made Nashville the capital of the genre. Hank Williams became the blueprint for the country singer-songwriter.
genres.listen: In Lovesick Blues you can hear two traditions meet: a Tin Pan Alley song from 1922 and the yodel of country music.

genres.name: Rhythm and blues
genres.text: After the Second World War big bands were too expensive to take on tour. Small line-ups with piano, electric guitar, bass, drums and one or two saxophones played loud, danceable music for an urban Black audience: rhythm and blues. Leiber and Stoller wrote Hound Dog for Big Mama Thornton in 1952; in 1953 the record spent seven weeks at number 1 on the R&B chart.
genres.listen: Listen to how Big Mama Thornton, raw and powerful, shows a man the door in Hound Dog.

genres.name: Rock 'n' roll
genres.text: Rock 'n' roll grew out of rhythm and blues, with influences from jump blues, boogie-woogie, gospel and country. You can recognise it by the backbeat on beats 2 and 4 and a guitar riff as the hook. Rocket 88 (1951) is often called the first rock 'n' roll record; Rock Around the Clock brought the style to a mass audience in 1955.
genres.listen: Notice the loud snare drum on 2 and 4 and, in Rocket 88, the distorted guitar coming from a damaged speaker.

genres.name: Rockabilly
genres.text: Rockabilly is the fast, stripped-down form of rock 'n' roll in which country and rhythm and blues come together. You can recognise it by the slapback echo on the voice, which defined the sound of Sun Records in Memphis, the slapped double bass and the metallic twang of the guitar. Elvis Presley, Gene Vincent and Eddie Cochran were the idols of the rockers in England and of the nozems, the teenage rebels of the Netherlands.
genres.listen: In That's All Right, can you hear the slapback echo and Bill Black's slapped double bass? In C'mon Everybody you hear the stop-time riff, in which the band falls silent and Cochran sings his line into the silence.

genres.name: Skiffle
genres.text: In the mid-1950s skiffle swept through Britain as a craze, with roots in American folk and blues; Lonnie Donegan had a hit with Rock Island Line in 1956. All you needed was a cheap guitar, a washboard and a tea-chest bass. Thousands of teenagers started a band this way, among them John Lennon with The Quarrymen.
genres.listen: In Rock Island Line, hear the simple line-up and the driving tempo: music that anyone could copy.

genres.name: British beat and the British Invasion
genres.text: After hundreds of hours in the clubs of Hamburg, The Beatles became the biggest band in Britain in 1963. From 1964 they, The Rolling Stones, The Animals and The Kinks conquered the American charts: the British Invasion. Bands such as The Who belonged to the mods of London.
genres.listen: In Please Please Me, hear how George Martin had a slow ballad sped up into a cheerful pop song.

mixtapes.heading: Hamburg: ruim 1.000 uur op het podium

genres.name: Folk revival
genres.text: In the 1950s and 1960s young white musicians in Greenwich Village, New York, rediscovered the old folk music: the folk revival. Dave Van Ronk made a new arrangement of House of the Rising Sun, which Bob Dylan put on his debut album in 1962. Dylan's protest songs later also inspired the Dutch singer Boudewijn de Groot.
genres.listen: Compare the descending bass line and minor chords of Van Ronk and Dylan with the modal version from 1933.

mixtapes.heading: House of the Rising Sun: zes versies

genres.name: Folk rock
genres.text: In folk rock, folk melodies are played on electric guitars. In 1965 The Byrds in Los Angeles played Dylan's Mr. Tambourine Man on a twelve-string electric guitar, and that same year Dylan himself went electric. Folk rock belonged to the hippies of the late 1960s; Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young brought the folk rock of California, with three and four voices in close harmony. From 2009 Mumford & Sons brought back the banjo and the acoustic guitar, and a few years later they were playing them in arenas.
genres.listen: In Our House, hear how closely the voices sit together: close harmony.

genres.name: Country rock
genres.text: At the end of the 1960s some rock musicians went back to the roots of American music; in 1968 The Byrds, with Gram Parsons, recorded Sweetheart of the Rodeo. The Rolling Stones recorded Wild Horses with a country influence from Gram Parsons, and Eagles from Los Angeles mixed rock with country. Hotel California (1977) ends with two guitars playing a solo together.
genres.listen: Listen to the end of Hotel California, where two guitars play the same solo in harmony.

genres.name: Indorock
genres.text: After 1949 Indo-Dutch people, who came to the Netherlands from the former Dutch East Indies, brought kroncong and the Hawaiian guitar with them; in the Netherlands this fused with American country and rock 'n' roll into indorock. It is fast, often instrumental guitar music with lots of echo and a wild stage show. The Tielman Brothers played in German clubs from 1959, a year before the Beatles arrived in Hamburg in 1960.
genres.listen: In Rock Little Baby of Mine, hear how an echo unit makes every fast guitar note ring on.

genres.name: Nederbeat
genres.text: Around the time of the Beatles' visit in June 1964, beat bands sprang up all over the Netherlands, with The Hague as the centre: the Golden Earrings, Q65, the Motions and Shocking Blue. Almost all of them sang in English; Cuby + Blizzards played heavy blues from the village of Grolloo. In February 1970 Shocking Blue's Venus became the first Dutch record to reach number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
genres.listen: Notice the simple guitar riff of Venus and the chorus you can sing along to after hearing it just once.

genres.name: Blues rock
genres.text: Cream, the trio of Eric Clapton, Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker, took the blues into the big halls, with long solos and loud amplifiers; Clapton played Robert Johnson's Cross Road Blues as Crossroads. Janis Joplin, too, sang the blues over loud, snarling rock guitars. Blues rock became the foundation of the hard rock of the 1970s.
genres.listen: In White Room, hear the intro in 5/4 time and the wah-wah pedal that makes the guitar 'talk'.

mixtapes.heading: De jaren 60: psychedelisch, acid en art

genres.name: Psychedelic rock
genres.text: Around 1966 and 1967 bands drew inspiration from Indian music, the classical avant-garde and LSD. You hear drones, modal sounds and studio effects; the Beatles used tape loops and sounds played backwards. San Francisco, with the Summer of Love of 1967, and London were the centres.
genres.listen: In White Rabbit, hear the march rhythm that keeps getting louder, with a Spanish, Phrygian sound.

tracks.title: Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds

mixtapes.heading: De jaren 60: psychedelisch, acid en art
Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
Strawberry Fields Forever: van demo tot plaat

genres.name: Art rock
genres.text: In New York, Lou Reed and John Cale's band The Velvet Underground worked with the artist Andy Warhol, who designed the cover with the banana. Cale had worked with the composer La Monte Young on long, sustained notes. The 1967 debut sold poorly at first, but went on to influence punk, postpunk and alternative rock.
genres.listen: In Venus in Furs, hear Cale's electric viola: a drone full of dissonance.

mixtapes.heading: De jaren 60: psychedelisch, acid en art

genres.name: Symphonic rock
genres.text: Symphonic rock brought classical music into pop: orchestras, church organ, Mellotron and themes by Bach or Beethoven. The organ part of Procol Harum's A Whiter Shade of Pale (1967) is inspired by Bach, and The Moody Blues recorded Days of Future Passed (1967) with an orchestra. In the Netherlands Ekseption played Beethoven's Fifth as a rock track, and groups such as Focus and Kayak made symphonic rock a Dutch speciality.
genres.listen: In A Whiter Shade of Pale, hear how the Hammond organ plays a melody that sounds like Baroque music, while the bass steps down note by note.

genres.name: Progressive rock
genres.text: Progressive rock turned the album into a composition, with long tracks, classical influences and complex time signatures. Yes's Close to the Edge (1972) fills an entire side of an album, and Pink Floyd's The Dark Side of the Moon (1973) is one continuous work. In the Netherlands Focus broke through with prog rock that had a sense of humour.
genres.listen: Count along in Money: the song is in seven beats, except during the guitar solo, with a tape loop of cash-register sounds as its rhythm.

genres.name: Hard rock and heavy metal
genres.text: Hard rock grew out of the blues rock of Cream, Jimi Hendrix and The Yardbirds. Led Zeppelin were formed in London in 1968, and Deep Purple and Black Sabbath laid the foundations of heavy metal. The guitar sounds distorted: what a sound engineer considered a fault became, for guitarists, a choice of tone.
genres.listen: Play the riff of Smoke on the Water yourself: fourths on G, B flat and C, the first thing beginner guitarists learn.

genres.name: Glam rock
genres.text: Around 1972 rock developed a theatrical side: costumes, make-up and a stage persona became just as important as the music. David Bowie invented Ziggy Stardust, a rock star from outer space, and became that character on stage and off it. The New Romantics of around 1980 drew heavily on glam rock.
genres.listen: Listen to how Bowie, in Ziggy Stardust, sings about a character rather than about himself.

genres.name: Krautrock
genres.text: In West Germany bands such as Can, Neu! and Kraftwerk looked for a sound of their own, free from American and British rock; English journalists called it krautrock. Neu! was founded by Michael Rother and Klaus Dinger, who had briefly played in Kraftwerk. Their motorik beat later resurfaced in postpunk, in electronic music and in the work of Radiohead.
genres.listen: In Hallogallo, hear how the drums keep the same 4/4 rhythm for minutes on end without fills, like a car at a constant speed.

genres.name: Southern rock
genres.text: Southern rock emerged in the southern United States around 1970, with The Allman Brothers Band as its pioneers. With Sweet Home Alabama (1974), Lynyrd Skynyrd from Jacksonville, Florida, wrote a reply to two songs by Neil Young. Thirty years later Kings of Leon started out in the same vein and scored a hit with Sex on Fire (2008).
genres.listen: Listen for the D-C-G riff of Sweet Home Alabama: the C is the flattened seventh degree of D, and that gives it the Mixolydian sound of blues and country.

genres.name: Heartland rock
genres.text: Bruce Springsteen from New Jersey made rock about ordinary people, work, cars and the dream of getting away. For Born to Run (1975) he built a wall of sound modelled on Phil Spector's Wall of Sound. Born in the U.S.A. (1984) sounds like a national anthem, but it is about a Vietnam veteran who cannot find work.
genres.listen: In Born to Run, try to pick out the layers: guitars, piano, organ, saxophone and glockenspiel.

genres.name: Punk
genres.text: Punk was the answer to rock that had become big, expensive and complicated: short, fast, loud songs with few chords, and the idea that anyone can start a band. The Ramones played at the New York club CBGB; in London there were the Sex Pistols and The Clash. Bands released records on small labels and fans made fanzines.
genres.listen: In Anarchy in the UK, hear the wall of guitars, recorded over one another several times.

genres.name: Postpunk
genres.text: Postpunk kept the energy and the do-it-yourself attitude of punk, but let go of the three chords. Joy Division from Manchester released their records on the local label Factory; in New York, Talking Heads showed that rock could be nervous, ironic and danceable. After the death of Ian Curtis in 1980, Joy Division carried on as New Order.
genres.listen: In She's Lost Control, hear how the bass plays the melody and the drums sound dry and almost mechanical.

genres.name: New wave
genres.text: New wave is an umbrella term for musicians who wanted to move on after punk, with more attention to atmosphere, melody and sound. Its roots lie in punk, but also in disco and krautrock. The movement runs from guitar bands such as The Cure, The Police and The Smiths to synth bands such as Tubeway Army and Depeche Mode.
genres.listen: In Are 'Friends' Electric?, hear the Minimoog and the Polymoog: it was one of the first British number 1 hits in which the synthesizer plays the leading role.

genres.name: Gothic rock
genres.text: Out of postpunk grew gothic rock: dark, echoing and slow. Bauhaus from Northampton recorded Bela Lugosi's Dead in 1979, nine minutes long and named after the actor who played Dracula. The Cure's A Forest appears on the album Seventeen Seconds (1980). The black clothes and dark hair of singer Robert Smith became the uniform of a new youth culture, the goths.
genres.listen: In A Forest, notice the guitar with its chorus effect and the bass that keeps repeating the same motif.

genres.name: Soft rock and AOR
genres.text: From the late 1960s radio stations on the FM band played whole album sides: album-oriented rock. Soft rock, with polished production and strong vocal melodies, was close to pop and could be heard from the early 1970s in the music of Carpenters, Bread and James Taylor; Fleetwood Mac's Rumours (1977) became one of the best-selling albums ever. In the 1980s AOR sounded slick and polished, with Toto and the power ballads of Foreigner.
genres.listen: In Africa, hear how drummer Jeff Porcaro plays a light, straight groove beneath layers of percussion.

tracks.title: I Want to Know What Love Is

genres.name: Glam metal and stadium rock
genres.text: After MTV launched in 1981, a rock band had to look good too. Glam metal combined hard rock with hairspray, make-up and tight trousers: pop songs dressed up as hard rock, with choruses made for stadiums. Bon Jovi and Van Halen scored big hits; in 1987 Guns N' Roses brought the rawness back.
genres.listen: In Livin' on a Prayer, hear the guitar played through a talk box and the key change in the final chorus.

genres.name: NWOBHM and thrash metal
genres.text: In the 1980s heavy metal became harder and faster. In England the New Wave of British Heavy Metal emerged around 1980, with Iron Maiden as its best-known band; in California Metallica played thrash metal, using downpicking. With producer Bob Rock, Metallica became radio-friendly in 1991.
genres.listen: In Run to the Hills, hear the galloping rhythm of the bass and drums and the two guitars playing side by side in thirds.

mixtapes.heading: De jaren 90: grunge en de rest

genres.name: Alternative rock
genres.text: Alongside the stadiums, a rock world of small labels, clubs and college radio grew up in the 1980s: alternative rock, known in America as college rock. Less virtuosic solos, less polished production and songs of their own. R.E.M. from Athens, Georgia, became big through college radio; U2 from Dublin grew into a stadium band.
genres.listen: In Sunday Bloody Sunday, hear the military pattern on the snare drum, and the violin.

tracks.title: It's the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine)

genres.name: Funk rock
genres.text: Living Colour from New York mixed hard rock with funk on Cult of Personality (1988); guitarist Vernon Reid was part of the Black Rock Coalition. The Red Hot Chili Peppers from Los Angeles combined funk with punk and rock. It was a return to the roots: rock 'n' roll had come out of Black music.
genres.listen: Listen to Give It Away and notice how bassist Flea slaps his strings and Anthony Kiedis raps more than he sings.

mixtapes.heading: De jaren 90: grunge en de rest

genres.name: Grunge
genres.text: Around the small label Sub Pop in Seattle, a scene emerged in the late 1980s that mixed punk and heavy metal into a raw, heavy sound. In January 1992, Nirvana's Nevermind knocked Michael Jackson's Dangerous off the top of the American album chart. Pearl Jam and Soundgarden also came from Seattle.
genres.listen: In Smells Like Teen Spirit, listen for the quiet-loud dynamics: soft verses and loud choruses on four power chords.

mixtapes.heading: De jaren 90: grunge en de rest

genres.name: Britpop
genres.text: Around 1993, British bands deliberately took a different direction from American grunge: back to the Beatles, The Kinks, The Who and the mods. In August 1995, Blur from London and Oasis from Manchester released a single on the same day. Blur won the battle for number one, Oasis the one for album sales.
genres.listen: Can you hear that Don't Look Back in Anger uses the chord sequence of Pachelbel's Canon, and that the piano intro quotes Imagine?

mixtapes.heading: Britpop, art rock en nu metal

genres.name: Nu metal
genres.text: Nu metal is metal combined with hip hop and electronics. Korn from Bakersfield released the first album in this style in 1994; around 2000, nu metal became popular. Linkin Park from Los Angeles had two vocalists: Chester Bennington sang and screamed, Mike Shinoda rapped. That rock was mixing with hip hop was a sign of things to come.
genres.listen: Listen to Numb and notice how heavy guitars come together with an electronic beat and synthesizers.

mixtapes.heading: Britpop, art rock en nu metal

genres.name: Boerenrock
genres.text: Normaal was founded in 1975 in the Achterhoek, a rural region in the east of the Netherlands, around singer Bennie Jolink, and sang in the local Achterhoek dialect. Oerend hard (1977) is about two drunken motorcyclists who ride home far too fast after a motocross race, with an accident as the result. The band performed in farmers' smocks and clogs; this music became known as boerenrock ('farmers' rock').
genres.listen: Put Oerend hard next to Radar Love by Golden Earring: two rock songs about the road that nobody would ever mix up.

genres.name: Dialect pop and rock
genres.text: From the 1980s onwards, more and more bands sang in their own regional language, not as a joke but to tell stories close to home about the village, the countryside and the family. Rowwen Hèze from America, a village in the north of Limburg, founded in 1985 around singer Jack Poels, mixed rock with folk and accordion. In Drenthe, Daniël Lohues sang in the Drents dialect with Skik. Normaal's boerenrock had shown that dialect could draw a large audience; with these bands the lyrics take centre stage and the music often sounds more acoustic and more melancholy.
genres.listen: Notice how the dialect colours the sound of the singing, and listen for the accordion and the acoustic instruments alongside guitar and drums.

genres.name: Rock in Dutch
genres.text: After Doe Maar, Dutch also became the language of rock. The Frank Boeijen Groep made new wave in their own language, De Dijk soul and rhythm and blues with horns, The Scene hard-hitting guitar rock and the Heideroosjes punk. They filled the new pop venues with audiences who knew the lyrics word for word.
genres.listen: Listen to Mag het licht uit and notice how De Dijk uses the warmth of a soul ballad for a Dutch lyric.

genres.name: Riot grrrl
genres.text: In the early 1990s, a feminist punk movement emerged in Olympia, in the state of Washington: riot grrrl. Bands such as Bikini Kill and Bratmobile saw the punk scene as a man's world; singer Kathleen Hanna called for 'girls to the front'. The bands made fanzines and released their records on small, independent labels.
genres.listen: Notice how simple Rebel Girl keeps things: a few chords, pounding drums and a lyric to scream along to.

genres.name: Brill Building and girl groups
genres.text: In the late 1950s, young songwriting duos such as Carole King and Gerry Goffin worked in small rooms with a piano in and around the Brill Building on Broadway, writing about what was on teenagers' minds. In 1961, Will You Love Me Tomorrow by The Shirelles became the first number one by a Black girl group. Many of those songs ended up with producer Phil Spector. He recorded them at the Gold Star studio in Los Angeles and piled up guitars, pianos, horns and strings into one dense wall of sound: the Wall of Sound, which you can hear in Be My Baby by The Ronettes (1963).
genres.listen: Listen for the Wall of Sound in Be My Baby: instruments doubled and tripled, drenched in reverb.

genres.name: Singer-songwriters
genres.text: Singer-songwriters wrote their own songs, sang them themselves and told of their own lives in the first person. Carole King moved from the Brill Building to Los Angeles; her Tapestry (1971) became one of the best-selling albums of the 1970s. Joni Mitchell tuned her guitar in dozens of open tunings.
genres.listen: In Big Yellow Taxi, listen for the bouncing guitar in open tuning beneath a lyric about the environment.

genres.name: Swedish pop (ABBA)
genres.text: ABBA won the Eurovision Song Contest in April 1974 with Waterloo. Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus wrote the music together, Björn wrote most of the English lyrics, and the voices of Agnetha and Frida were recorded several times on top of each other. From the 1970s onwards, Sweden built a hit industry of its own.
genres.listen: Notice that Dancing Queen does not start with a verse but with part of the chorus: the strongest moment comes straight away.

genres.name: New Romantic
genres.text: In the late 1970s, you only got into the London club Blitz if you looked striking. Out of that scene came New Romantic, a movement within new wave that leans on glam rock, with make-up, historical costumes and gender bending. Duran Duran shot expensive videos and stood at the start of the Second British Invasion via MTV.
genres.listen: In Fade to Grey, listen for the whispered French phrases over a pulsing sequencer bass.

genres.name: Neue Deutsche Welle
genres.text: Around 1979, a wave of German-language rock and pop grew out of punk and new wave in West Germany, which journalist Alfred Hilsberg called Neue Deutsche Welle ('New German Wave'). It began in the avant-garde with DAF and Einstürzende Neubauten and reached the charts within a few years. The Austrian Falco also scored in that wave, with Der Kommissar. By around 1985 the genre had vanished.
genres.listen: Can you hear how cheerful 99 Luftballons sounds, even though it is a protest song against the Cold War?

genres.name: British Eurobeat (Stock Aitken Waterman)
genres.text: In the mid-1980s, a new pop sound emerged in England out of Italo disco and Hi-NRG: British Eurobeat. The production trio Stock Aitken Waterman worked like a factory: the same studio, the same musicians, only the singers changed. More than a hundred Top 40 hits came out of their London studio.
genres.listen: In You Spin Me Round, listen for the Hi-NRG bass in eighth notes.

mixtapes.heading: British Eurobeat en Stock Aitken Waterman

genres.name: Boy bands and girl groups
genres.text: Every decade has its teen idol, with a recognisable face, a simple hook and a production that suits the medium; the 1990s brought the cast boy band and girl group. The Spice Girls were put together in 1994 through auditions after an advertisement, and became a brand. Wannabe was number one in Britain in 1996 and in the United States in 1997.
genres.listen: Listen to Wannabe and notice how the voices take turns, so that each member gets a role of her own.

genres.name: Stockholm pop (Max Martin)
genres.text: At the Cheiron Studio in Stockholm, Max Martin and his colleagues wrote and produced the hits of the Backstreet Boys, *NSYNC and Britney Spears from the mid-1990s onwards. Martin works with 'melodic math': lines with the same number of syllables, vowels that sing well on the high notes and a hook that keeps coming back. Later he wrote for artists including Taylor Swift and The Weeknd.
genres.listen: ...Baby One More Time opens with three heavy piano notes and then the voice straight away: notice how the hook lands within the first few seconds.

mixtapes.heading: Van AABA naar couplet en refrein

genres.name: Kleinkunst
genres.text: Kleinkunst ('small art') is the Dutch-language song from cabaret and theatre, with the lyrics at the centre and a small accompaniment; in the 1950s, Wim Sonneveld, Toon Hermans and Jules de Corte were the big names. Around 1965 that tradition moved towards pop, when Boudewijn de Groot sang songs to lyrics by Lennaert Nijgh, inspired by American folk and Bob Dylan. In the 1980s, Klein Orkest brought kleinkunst together with a pop band.
genres.listen: Listen to Over de muur and notice how a narrative song about East and West Berlin arrives at a chorus that everyone sings along to.

genres.name: Nederpop
genres.text: Nederpop is the umbrella term for Dutch pop music. In the early 1980s, bands that sang in their own language broke through: the Dutch counterpart of the Neue Deutsche Welle. Doe Maar played ska and reggae with Dutch lyrics and broke through on a massive scale in 1982; Het Goede Doel made synthpop and the Frank Boeijen Groep new wave. Singing in Dutch had now become ordinary pop, in the charts as well.
genres.listen: In Sinds 1 dag of 2 (32 jaar), listen for the ska rhythm with the guitar on the offbeat.

genres.name: Dutch-language song
genres.text: In the 1990s, the Dutch-language song grew to reach a large audience: from 1994 onwards, Marco Borsato had hit after hit with ballads. Acda en de Munnik continued the kleinkunst tradition, and BLØF made Zoutelande (2017) with Geike Arnaert, one of the biggest hits ever in the Netherlands. Around 2020, Snelle and Froukje found their audience through TikTok and YouTube.
genres.listen: Listen to Zoutelande: a calm duet about a beach in Zeeland.

genres.name: Streaming pop
genres.text: Streaming pop is pop made for the way people have listened since the 2010s: through Spotify, YouTube and TikTok. Songs have become shorter on average, often start straight away with the hook and mix genres freely. In December 2018, Lil Nas X from Atlanta put Old Town Road online, over a beat he had bought for 30 dollars. The song took off on TikTok, where thousands of users made videos to it, and spent nineteen weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100. The debate over whether it was country showed how genres blur into one another in the streaming era.
genres.listen: Listen for the country banjo over a trap beat with deep 808 bass and rattling hi-hats.

mixtapes.heading: TikTok en het einde van genres

genres.name: Soul
genres.text: Soul emerged in the mid-1950s from gospel, jazz and rhythm and blues. In 1954, with I Got a Woman, Ray Charles took the step from church to the charts, on the melody of a gospel song. Soul became the soundtrack of the civil rights movement; Aretha Franklin's Respect became a song for civil rights and women's rights at the same time.
genres.listen: In Respect, listen for the melisma and for the call and response between Aretha and the backing singers, the form of the church service.

mixtapes.heading: Soul: de kerk gaat de straat op

genres.name: Motown
genres.text: In 1959, Berry Gordy started a label in Detroit that he organised like a car factory, with staff songwriters, the house band The Funk Brothers and a weekly quality control meeting. The aim was Black music that white audiences would buy too: 'The Sound of Young America'. The Supremes scored twelve number-one hits; in 1972 Motown moved to Los Angeles.
genres.listen: Listen for the tambourine on the beat and the restless bass line of James Jamerson.

genres.name: Stax and Memphis soul
genres.text: In Memphis, Jim Stewart started the label Satellite in 1957; his sister Estelle Axton joined a year later, and from 1961 it was called Stax (STewart + AXton). Recording was done live in an old cinema, and the sound was rawer and more Southern than Motown: a heavy bass, dry drums and the Memphis Horns. The house band Booker T. & the MG's was made up of Black and white musicians.
genres.listen: Green Onions is a 12-bar blues in F: listen for the repeated figure on the Hammond organ and the sharp guitar chords cutting against it.

tracks.title: (Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay

genres.name: Funk
genres.text: Funk grew out of jazz, rhythm and blues and soul in the second half of the 1960s, with James Brown in the leading role. All the instruments come together on the first beat, 'on the one', and rhythm comes before harmony: a song often stays on a single chord for minutes on end. George Clinton with P-Funk, Stevie Wonder and Earth, Wind & Fire built on it.
genres.listen: In Sex Machine, listen for the short, muted guitar stroke, the bass of Bootsy Collins and the call and response between Brown and Bobby Byrd.

tracks.title: Get Up (I Feel Like Being a) Sex Machine

genres.name: Disco
genres.text: Disco emerged around 1970 in New York clubs for Black, Latino and gay audiences, such as The Loft and later the Paradise Garage, where the DJ blended records seamlessly into one another. The rhythm is four-on-the-floor: a bass drum on every beat, at around 120 bpm, with strings and horns on top. After Disco Demolition Night in 1979, disco lived on as garage and house.
genres.listen: In Le Freak, listen for Nile Rodgers' short 'chucking' chords and Bernard Edwards' bass, which never stops moving.

genres.name: Contemporary R&B
genres.text: The term rhythm and blues returned as R&B: vocals, production and drum machines take centre stage, and the producer becomes a star. It started with Michael Jackson and Quincy Jones; Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis brought Prince's Minneapolis sound to Janet Jackson (Control, 1986). By way of new jack swing and hip hop soul, R&B and hip hop became the core of the mainstream after 2000.
genres.listen: Listen to I Wanna Dance with Somebody: a gospel voice in a synthpop production.

genres.name: Neo-soul
genres.text: Neo-soul is R&B that reached back to the soul of the 1970s, with Erykah Badu and D'Angelo among others. Badu recorded Tyrone (1997) live, with harmonies from jazz, and the warm sound of the Rhodes piano returned too. On her solo album (1998), Lauryn Hill combined doo-wop backing vocals, a soul groove and rap.
genres.listen: Can you hear that Tyrone was recorded live, with jazz harmonies beneath the voice?

genres.name: Early hip hop
genres.text: On 11 August 1973, Kool Herc, who knew the sound systems of Kingston, played records at a party on Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx. With two copies of the same record he extended the break, and MCs began rapping over it. The first rap hit was Rapper's Delight (1979); The Message (1982) was the first rap hit to describe life in the ghetto.
genres.listen: In The Message, listen for the slow tempo, the menacing mood and the synthesizer line that keeps coming back.

genres.name: Electro
genres.text: Afrika Bambaataa also played Kraftwerk at his parties in the Bronx. In 1982, with Arthur Baker and John Robie, he recorded Planet Rock: the melody from Trans-Europe Express and a rhythm modelled on Kraftwerk's Numbers, programmed on the Roland TR-808. That is how electro was born: cold European synthesizers with an American breakbeat.
genres.listen: Listen to the 808: a short, dry snare, a ticking hi-hat and a deep bass drum that rings on for a long time.

genres.name: Golden age hip hop
genres.text: In the late 1980s, samplers became affordable and producers built beats from fragments of existing recordings: the golden age of hip hop. Public Enemy piled up samples, sirens and scratches, De La Soul chose a playful tone and the Wu-Tang Clan lo-fi beats with samples from kung fu films. After a lawsuit against Biz Markie in 1991, it became standard practice to ask permission and pay for every sample.
genres.listen: In Night of the Living Baseheads, listen to how The Bomb Squad stacks layer upon layer: samples, sirens, scratches and speeches.

genres.name: Gangsta rap
genres.text: Gangsta rap took shape on the West Coast. After forerunners such as Schoolly D from Philadelphia and Ice-T from Los Angeles, N.W.A. from Compton, a suburb of Los Angeles, released Straight Outta Compton in 1988, with Fuck tha Police as an indictment of police violence. Lyrics about violence caused an uproar. In the mid-1990s the rivalry between the East Coast and the West Coast got out of hand; 2Pac (1996) and The Notorious B.I.G. (1997) were shot dead.
genres.listen: Listen to how directly and explicitly the lyrics indict the Los Angeles police.

genres.name: G-funk
genres.text: Dr. Dre, a former member of N.W.A., developed G-funk with The Chronic (1992): slow grooves with samples from George Clinton's P-Funk, a high synthesizer line and lots of space. On California Love, Roger Troutman sings through a talk box. Later Dre chose a barer sound: Still D.R.E. (1999) revolves around a minimal piano riff by Scott Storch.
genres.listen: In Nuthin' but a "G" Thang, listen for the slow funk groove, the high synthesizer line and Snoop Dogg's relaxed flow. Compare that with the silence around the piano riff in Still D.R.E.

tracks.artist: Dr. Dre feat. Snoop Doggy Dogg
tracks.title: Nuthin' but a "G" Thang

genres.name: Trap
genres.text: From the early 2000s, trap grew up in Atlanta: a hip hop style from the South of the United States, named after the trap house where drugs were sold. T.I., Young Jeezy and Gucci Mane were the first names. Its foundation is long, gliding 808 bass drums and fast hi-hat rolls, and Auto-Tune became an ordinary part of the voice. Old Town Road (2018) showed how trap could blend with country.
genres.listen: In What You Know, listen for the deep 808 bass and the hi-hats rattling in fast rolls.

genres.name: Nederhop
genres.text: From 1990, Osdorp Posse from Amsterdam rapped in broad Amsterdam dialect: hardcore rap about the street and the city. In 1995, Extince from Oosterhout scored the first Dutch-language hip hop hit with Spraakwater. After 2000, Nederhop (Dutch hip hop) grew into one of the most important genres in the country, with De Jeugd van Tegenwoordig and Typhoon among others.
genres.listen: Listen to Spraakwater and notice how smoothly the Dutch rhymes and swings over a relaxed funk beat.

genres.name: Moog and the first synthesizer pop
genres.text: From 1964, in Trumansburg, Robert Moog built synthesizers from separate modules that you connected with cables. An oscillator makes a tone, a filter removes overtones from it, and an envelope determines how the tone starts and fades away. The modules control one another with electrical voltage. In 1968 Wendy Carlos showed what the instrument could do with Switched-On Bach, and the album was a huge success. After that, rock bands used the Moog for solos and new tone colours. The characteristic sound lies mainly in the filter, which lets a tone 'open up'.
genres.listen: Can you hear a tone that opens up from dull to bright? That is the Moog's filter.

mixtapes.heading: De eerste vrouwen achter de knoppen
Abbey Road: nog één keer zoals vroeger

genres.name: Kraftwerk and the man-machine
genres.text: Kraftwerk was founded in 1970 in Düsseldorf and set aside guitar and drum kit for synthesizers, electronic drums and the vocoder. Autobahn (1974) opens with a 22-minute track about a drive along the motorway; Trans-Europe Express (1977) sounds like wheels on rails. Its influence reached as far as hip hop in New York and techno in Detroit.
genres.listen: In Trans-Europe Express, listen for the tight rhythm without swing, like a train on the rails.

genres.name: Synth disco and Hi-NRG
genres.text: In Munich in 1977, producer Giorgio Moroder made I Feel Love with Donna Summer, without a band: the bass line comes from a Moog driven by a sequencer. The song stands at the start of Hi-NRG, Italo disco and later house. Hi-NRG itself took shape in the early 1980s in gay clubs in San Francisco, New York and London: fast, electronic dance music, with producers such as Patrick Cowley and Bobby Orlando.
genres.listen: Listen for the bass line that a sequencer repeats endlessly and exactly in time, with the high, long-held vocals above it.

tracks.title: You Spin Me Round (Like a Record)

genres.name: Synthpop
genres.text: Synthpop is the poppiest branch of new wave: Kraftwerk was the model for Gary Numan, OMD and The Human League, and later for the Pet Shop Boys. It is often a duo of a singer and someone behind the synthesizers. Eurythmics recorded most of Sweet Dreams themselves, in an attic studio in north London, with a drum machine that also drove the bass line, and Bronski Beat sang openly about life as a gay man.
genres.listen: Listen to Tainted Love and notice how a soul song from 1964 is given a cold, electronic makeover.

mixtapes.heading: Take On Me: vijf jaar werk aan één riff

genres.name: Italo disco
genres.text: Italy developed its own electronic dance music, a blend of synthpop and Eurodisco, with Giorgio Moroder as its great forerunner. Producers released solo projects under invented names, with English lyrics sung in an Italian accent. Arpeggiators and vocoders define the sound.
genres.listen: Listen to Dolce Vita and notice the bass in eighth notes from an arpeggiator, like an engine that never stops.

genres.name: Detroit techno
genres.text: In Belleville, near Detroit, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson grew up with the radio show of The Electrifying Mojo, who played Parliament alongside Kraftwerk. Atkins started out in 1981 with Cybotron and in 1985, as Model 500, released No UFO's. Derrick May described techno as George Clinton and Kraftwerk stuck in a lift together.
genres.listen: Listen to Strings of Life and notice the strings and piano coming from a sampler, and the intro without a bass drum.

genres.name: House
genres.text: From 1977 Frankie Knuckles played a mix of disco, soul and European synthpop at The Warehouse in Chicago, for a crowd that was mostly Black and gay. From 1984 young producers in Chicago began making their own tracks with a drum machine, a synthesizer and a tape recorder. At its core, house is disco made by a machine: four-on-the-floor at around 120 bpm.
genres.listen: Listen to Your Love and notice the bass drum on every beat beneath a synthesizer line that keeps coming back.

tracks.title: Move Your Body (The House Music Anthem)

genres.name: Acid house
genres.text: On Acid Tracks (1987) the Chicago group Phuture turned the knobs of a Roland TB-303, a flopped bass-line machine, while it was playing. As the filter is opened and closed, the bass line squeaks, crackles and wails: acid house. The sound crossed the ocean and in England became the music of the first raves.
genres.listen: Follow the bass line in Acid Tracks and notice how it changes as the filter is opened and closed.

mixtapes.heading: De TB-303: een flop wordt acid

genres.name: Rave
genres.text: In 1987 English DJs came back from Ibiza and started clubs playing acid house; the summers of 1988 and 1989 became the Second Summer of Love. Parties moved to warehouses and fields, until a law in 1994 gave the police the power to shut them down. Out of rave came jungle, drum and bass, big beat and IDM.
genres.listen: Listen to Pump Up the Volume and notice how a track is built from dozens of samples of other records.

genres.name: Eurodance
genres.text: In the early nineties the European mainland danced to Eurodance: a solid house beat, a rapped verse and a sung chorus. Producers in Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Italy used it to build short pop songs. 2 Unlimited had Dutch faces and Belgian producers; in 1993 No Limit was number 1 in much of Europe.
genres.listen: Listen to No Limit and notice the construction kit: a recurring synth riff, a rapped verse, a chorus that is little more than the title, and a break.

genres.name: Gabber and happy hardcore
genres.text: In the early nineties gabber emerged in Rotterdam: hardcore at 160 to more than 200 bpm, with a distorted bass drum that sounds like a hammer. From 1992 the Thunderdome parties run by ID&T drew thousands of visitors. Happy hardcore made the sound lighter, with cheerful melodies and high-pitched voices, and scored hits in the Dutch Top 40.
genres.listen: Listen to Poing and notice the hard, distorted bass drum of early gabber, and in Wonderful Days (1994) the high tempo and cheerful melody of happy hardcore.

genres.name: Dutch trance
genres.text: Around 2000 trance became a Dutch export product. DJs such as Tiësto, Armin van Buuren and Ferry Corsten played all over the world, and in 2004 Tiësto performed at the opening of the Olympic Games in Athens. ID&T organised Sensation in the Amsterdam ArenA.
genres.listen: Notice the long build-up to the moment when the beat comes back in.

genres.name: French house
genres.text: From the mid-nineties producers in France such as Daft Punk, Cassius and Étienne de Crécy made French house: house tracks with filters and samples from old disco and funk. On Around the World (1997) a single short phrase is repeated over and over, while the accompaniment changes around the voice.
genres.listen: Listen to what changes in the accompaniment while the title keeps coming back.

genres.name: EDM
genres.text: Around 2010 electronic dance music became the big new genre in the United States, under the name EDM. Festivals drew hundreds of thousands of visitors and the DJ became a pop star with a light show of their own. Avicii built Levels on a vocal sample of Etta James, and Martin Garrix made Animals on a laptop in his bedroom.
genres.listen: Listen to the build-up and the drop: the moment when the beat and the bass kick back in.

genres.name: Trip hop
genres.text: Trip hop is a form of downtempo from the Bristol producer scene, where sound systems mixed reggae, hip hop, soul and punk. Massive Attack grew out of the collective The Wild Bunch. Slow, heavy breakbeats, samples from old records, a deep reggae bass and vocals that are more about atmosphere than story.
genres.listen: Listen to Unfinished Sympathy and notice the slow beat beneath strings and a voice that creates atmosphere.

genres.name: Electronic studio and musique concrète
genres.text: In 1948 Pierre Schaeffer in Paris made music out of recorded sounds: musique concrète. In 1951 the broadcaster WDR in Cologne set up a studio for electronic music, with oscillators, filters and tape recorders; Karlheinz Stockhausen composed there with scissors and sticky tape. And at Philips in Eindhoven, Dick Raaijmakers and Tom Dissevelt were at work. Ten years later these tape techniques found their way into pop music.
genres.listen: Listen to Gesang der Jünglinge and notice how a boy's voice merges with electronic sounds.

genres.name: Radiophonic Workshop
genres.text: From 1958 the BBC had its own department for electronic sound, the Radiophonic Workshop, which made sounds and music for radio and television. In 1963 Delia Derbyshire built the Doctor Who theme, composed by Ron Grainer, note by note out of oscillators, noise and tape loops. The staff worked anonymously.
genres.listen: The bass line of Doctor Who was made from a single plucked string, cut again and again at a different pitch.

mixtapes.heading: De eerste vrouwen achter de knoppen

genres.name: Synthesizer orchestra, ambient and new age
genres.text: Jean-Michel Jarre, who had worked with Pierre Schaeffer, recorded Oxygène in 1976 in a home studio in Paris. Vangelis, based in London, wrote film music such as Chariots of Fire, and Kitaro in Japan made beatless music for the series Silk Road. Tangerine Dream and Klaus Schulze in Berlin had gone before them, and in 1978, with Music for Airports, Brian Eno gave the genre its name: ambient.
genres.listen: Listen to Oxygène and notice the cheap Korg rhythm box beneath simple melodies that stick in your head.

genres.name: Ska, rocksteady and reggae
genres.text: In Kingston, sound systems played American rhythm and blues; when those records became scarce, Jamaican producers started recording their own. That is how ska, rocksteady and, around 1968, reggae arose one after another, with drums and bass as the riddim and the guitar's skank on 2 and 4. Bob Marley became one of the first global stars from what was then called the Third World, and producers such as King Tubby turned it into dub.
genres.listen: Listen to Stir It Up and notice the one drop: the bass drum falls on the third beat and the first beat is left empty.

genres.name: 2 Tone
genres.text: Around 1969 the first skinheads adopted the ska and reggae of Jamaican migrants. In 1979 Jerry Dammers founded the 2 Tone label in Coventry, with often deliberately mixed bands that played ska with the energy of punk: The Specials, The Selecter and The Beat. Madness also started out on the label. Ghost Town (1981) is about towns emptying out because of unemployment.
genres.listen: Listen to Ghost Town and notice the slow ska rhythm on the offbeat, the minor chords and the horns that call the Middle East to mind.

genres.name: Bebop
genres.text: In the early forties young jazz musicians held jam sessions at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem after their work in the big bands. That is where bebop was born: music for musicians, often at very fast tempos, sometimes above 250 bpm, with rapid chord changes and long solos. Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie led the way; in Paris and Amsterdam it became the music of the artistic crowd.
genres.listen: Anthropology is a contrafact: a new melody on the chords of I Got Rhythm.

genres.name: Latin jazz
genres.text: From 1943 Machito and Mario Bauzá mixed jazz with Cuban music in New York. In 1947 Dizzy Gillespie took the Cuban conguero Chano Pozo, who had recently settled in New York, into his big band. Jazz swings long-short, while Afro-Cuban music is built on evenly divided notes and the clave; in Latin jazz the two come together. From 1958 João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim created bossa nova in Rio de Janeiro.
genres.listen: Listen to Manteca and notice Pozo's conga ostinato and a bebop bridge in swing: two rhythmic worlds in one piece.

genres.name: Cool Jazz and modal jazz
genres.text: In 1949 and 1950 Miles Davis recorded with a nonet the sessions that were later called Birth of the Cool, with French horn and tuba alongside the usual horns and arrangements by Gil Evans, among others. Cool Jazz is soft, with little vibrato and plenty of space. With Kind of Blue (1959) Davis took the step to modal jazz; it became the best-selling jazz album ever.
genres.listen: Listen to Blue in Green and notice the soft trumpet tone with little vibrato and plenty of space between the notes.

genres.name: West Coast jazz
genres.text: In the fifties Cool Jazz developed its own variant in California, played by musicians who also worked in the film and television studios. In 1952 in Los Angeles Gerry Mulligan started a pianoless quartet with Chet Baker, so that baritone sax and trumpet play in counterpoint. Dave Brubeck's quartet from San Francisco recorded Time Out in 1959, with Take Five by saxophonist Paul Desmond.
genres.listen: Count along to Take Five: it is in five beats, divided into three plus two.

genres.name: Hard bop
genres.text: On the East Coast many Black musicians found Cool Jazz too restrained. Hard bop uses the harmony and solo technique of bebop, but mixes them with rhythm and blues, gospel and blues, over a heavier groove. Much of it was released on the New York label Blue Note, such as John Coltrane's Blue Train (1957).
genres.listen: Listen to Blue Train and notice the heavy groove and the bluesy theme the horns play together.

genres.name: Free jazz
genres.text: Free jazz let go of the agreements about theme, chord progression, time signature and tempo: musicians often improvise at the same time and dissonance becomes raw material. The name comes from the album Free Jazz (1961) by Ornette Coleman from Texas, who arrived in New York from Los Angeles at the end of 1959 with a pianoless quartet.
genres.listen: Listen to Lonely Woman and notice how the horns play the melody together, without a piano and without a fixed chord progression.

genres.name: Fusion and jazz rock
genres.text: Miles Davis listened to Jimi Hendrix, Sly and the Family Stone and James Brown, and played electric instruments on In a Silent Way (1969) and, on Bitches Brew (1970), several drummers at once as well. Fusion is the merging of jazz and rock, in which the swing largely disappears. Steely Dan used jazz chords in pop songs, recorded with the finest session musicians.
genres.listen: Listen to Birdland and notice how the groove runs straight instead of swinging.

genres.name: Smooth jazz
genres.text: In the mid-seventies a softer variant of fusion emerged, which became hugely popular in the eighties. Smooth jazz borrows from soul and funk: a relaxed groove, warm chords and a melody on saxophone, guitar or electric piano, with a polished production. George Benson and Grover Washington Jr. were well-known names.
genres.listen: Listen to Just the Two of Us and notice the relaxed groove beneath the saxophone and the voice of Bill Withers.

tracks.title: Just the Two of Us (met Bill Withers)

genres.name: Nu jazz
genres.text: In London from the late eighties DJs such as Gilles Peterson played acid jazz: jazz, funk and soul for the dance floor. Hip hop producers searched old jazz, soul and funk records for breaks to sample; in 1993 Us3 made Cantaloop on a sample of Herbie Hancock. Out of that meeting between jazz and club culture came nu jazz: an electronic form of jazz, combined with house, downtempo and breakbeat.
genres.listen: Listen to So Flute and notice how a jazz flute plays over a house beat.

genres.name: Bluegrass
genres.text: From the forties a fast, acoustic variant emerged within country: bluegrass, named after the band of mandolin player Bill Monroe from Kentucky, the Blue Grass Boys. In 1945 banjo player Earl Scruggs from North Carolina joined that band. He played with three fingers, in fast patterns of eight notes per bar: the rolls. In 1948 Scruggs and singer-guitarist Lester Flatt started a band of their own; their Foggy Mountain Breakdown (1949) was later heard in the film Bonnie and Clyde (1967).
genres.listen: Listen to Foggy Mountain Breakdown and notice the banjo: three fingers, rolls of eight notes per bar, while fiddle and guitar hold the tempo.

tracks.artist: Bill Monroe & His Blue Grass Boys
tracks.title: Blue Moon of Kentucky
I'm a Man of Constant Sorrow

genres.name: Bossa nova
genres.text: In Rio de Janeiro, guitarist and singer João Gilberto and composer Antônio Carlos Jobim created bossa nova from 1958: a soft, restrained version of samba, with jazz chords and a voice that almost whispers. Bossa nova is Brazilian, not Afro-Cuban; the rhythm is different, and so is the mood. Through the American saxophonist Stan Getz the style became popular in the United States: Getz/Gilberto (1964), with The Girl from Ipanema sung by Astrud Gilberto, became a hit far beyond the jazz audience.
genres.listen: Listen to The Girl from Ipanema and notice the soft bossa rhythm on the guitar, the jazz chords and the singing that almost whispers, followed by Stan Getz's saxophone.

tracks.artist: Stan Getz & João Gilberto met Astrud Gilberto
tracks.title: The Girl from Ipanema

genres.name: Doo-wop
genres.text: Doo-wop is harmony singing from the rhythm and blues of the fifties. Groups of four or five singers rehearsed on street corners in cities such as New York: a lead singer, with a small backing chorus beneath him singing sounds and syllables instead of words. Many doo-wop ballads are in 12/8, with a slow, swaying rhythm. The style left its mark on the girl groups, on the early Beatles and later on the backing vocals of Lauryn Hill.
genres.listen: Listen to Earth Angel and notice the backing chorus beneath the lead voice and the swaying rhythm in 12/8, in which every beat is divided into three.

tracks.title: In Spite of All the Danger
In the Still of the Nite

genres.name: March music and brass bands
genres.text: By the end of the nineteenth century almost every American town had a brass band, and John Philip Sousa, leader of the United States Marine Band in Washington, wrote marches such as The Stars and Stripes Forever (1896). A march is in 2/4, with the weight on 1 and 3, and consists of several melodies in a row, the strains. Ragtime took over that time signature and form, and in New Orleans brass bands played at funerals: a slow hymn on the way to the cemetery, cheerful music on the way back.
genres.listen: Listen to The Stars and Stripes Forever and notice the strict two-beat pulse and the melodies taking turns, as they later would in ragtime.

tracks.artist: United States Marine Band (John Philip Sousa)
tracks.title: The Stars and Stripes Forever
Just a Little While to Stay Here

genres.name: Habanera
genres.text: The habanera is a nineteenth-century Cuban dance, named after Havana. Its hallmark is the rhythm in 2/4 with a dotted first beat and an accent that falls just off the beat. Via Spain and via the ports of the Caribbean that rhythm spread throughout the Americas: in New Orleans you can hear it in early jazz, and it also lies beneath the Afro-Cuban music of Latin jazz.
genres.listen: Listen to La Paloma and notice the swaying habanera rhythm in the accompaniment: long, short and then two equal beats.

tracks.title: Carmen: L'amour est un oiseau rebelle (Habanera)

genres.name: Boogie-woogie
genres.text: Boogie-woogie is a piano style that grew out of the blues, played in bars and at house parties in the South and later in Chicago. The left hand plays a fast, repeated bass pattern of eight notes per bar, the right hand riffs and blue notes. Pine Top Smith recorded Pine Top's Boogie Woogie in 1928; in the late thirties the style became a craze, and the rolling left hand returned in rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll.
genres.listen: Listen to Pine Top's Boogie Woogie and notice the left hand playing the same rolling bass pattern over and over, while Smith calls out the dance steps.

genres.name: Jump blues
genres.text: Jump blues is the swing of a small band with horns: fast shuffles, boogie-woogie on the piano and a singer who entertains the audience. In the forties Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five scored one hit after another with it, such as Caldonia (1945). Rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll grew out of jump blues.
genres.listen: Listen to Caldonia and notice the shuffle of the small band, the saxophone and the shouts of Louis Jordan.

tracks.artist: Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five
tracks.title: Caldonia

genres.name: Chicago blues
genres.text: After the Second World War many Black Americans moved from the South to Chicago, and the blues went with them. Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf played it electric, with guitar, harmonica, piano, bass and drums, and recorded for the Chess label. Because a whole band had to change chords at the same time, the 12-bar pattern became the standard. British bands such as The Rolling Stones, named after a Muddy Waters song, built on it.
genres.listen: Listen to Hoochie Coochie Man and notice the stop-time riff: the band plays a short figure and falls silent, and in that silence Muddy Waters sings.

genres.name: Son
genres.text: Son comes from the east of Cuba and became popular in Havana in the twenties. It mixes Spanish song forms and the tres, a Cuban guitar, with African rhythms and percussion: bongos, maracas and the clave. A singer alternates with a chorus, and in the second part the band repeats a short pattern, the montuno. Mambo, salsa and much of Latin jazz grew out of son.
genres.listen: Listen to Chan Chan and notice the tres, the tapping of the clave and the chorus answering the singer.

genres.name: Mambo
genres.text: Mambo grew out of danzón and son in Havana in the late thirties. From 1949 pianist and bandleader Dámaso Pérez Prado turned it into a craze in Mexico City, with a big band that had the brass play sharp and high. In the early fifties thousands of people in New York were dancing the mambo too, among other places at the Palladium Ballroom.
genres.listen: Listen to Mambo No. 5 and notice the blazing trumpets, the saxophones playing against the beat and the cries of Pérez Prado.

tracks.title: Cherry Pink and Apple Blossom White

genres.name: Cha-cha-chá
genres.text: The cha-cha-chá is a slower offshoot of the mambo that is easier to dance to, devised by violinist Enrique Jorrín of the Orquesta América in Havana. La Engañadora (1953) is regarded as the first number. The name comes from the shuffle of the feet on the three quick steps.
genres.listen: Count along in La Engañadora to the three quick steps at the end of every bar: cha-cha-chá.

genres.name: Salsa
genres.text: Salsa is the name that emerged in New York in the late 1960s for the Afro-Cuban dance music of Puerto Rican and Cuban musicians. The Fania label, with Johnny Pacheco, Willie Colón, Héctor Lavoe and Celia Cruz, made salsa big in the 1970s. Its foundation is the son, with the clave and the montuno, enriched with trombones, jazz chords and lyrics about life in the barrio.
genres.listen: Listen to El Cantante and notice the steady clave pattern beneath the trombones and the free-flowing vocals of Héctor Lavoe.

genres.name: Merengue
genres.text: Merengue is the national dance of the Dominican Republic: fast music in 2/4 with accordion, the tambora, a two-headed drum, and the güira, a metal scraper. In the 1930s, under the dictator Trujillo, merengue became the country's official dance music. In the late 1980s Juan Luis Guerra brought it to an international audience, with jazz and pop influences.
genres.listen: Listen to Ojalá Que Llueva Café: can you hear the fast rhythm of the tambora and güira beneath the vocal harmonies?

tracks.artist: Johnny Ventura y Su Combo Show
tracks.title: Patacón Pisao

genres.name: Samba
genres.text: Samba was born in the Afro-Brazilian neighbourhoods of Rio de Janeiro; Pelo Telefone (1917) is regarded as the first recorded samba. The music is in 2/4 and driven by percussion, and from the 1930s onwards samba became the music of carnival and of the radio. In 1958 João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim created a soft, understated version of it: bossa nova.
genres.listen: Listen to Aquarela do Brasil and notice the samba rhythm in the percussion, beneath a large orchestra.

genres.name: Dub
genres.text: In Kingston, producers made an instrumental version without vocals for the B-side of their singles. Engineer King Tubby went further: in his small studio he dropped instruments in and out on the mixing desk, added long echo and reverb, and filtered the sound. In this way an existing recording was turned into a new track: dub. The mixing desk was his instrument. Ideas from dub, such as space, a heavy bass and the remix, returned in hip hop, jungle, trip hop and dubstep.
genres.listen: Notice what drops out and comes back: which instrument disappears into the echo, and when?

tracks.artist: Johnny Clarke, King Tubby & The Aggrovators
tracks.title: A Ruffer Dub

genres.name: Dancehall
genres.text: Dancehall emerged in Jamaica in the 1980s, named after the dance venues where sound systems played. Deejays, which in Jamaica means the artists on the microphone, talk and sing over riddims; from Under Mi Sleng Teng (1985) onwards, those riddims were increasingly made digitally. Yellowman and later Shabba Ranks became the stars.
genres.listen: Listen to Mr. Loverman and notice the deep voice of Shabba Ranks over a digital riddim.

genres.name: Raga rock
genres.text: In the mid-1960s Western bands began to use Indian instruments and scales: raga rock. George Harrison played sitar on The Beatles' Norwegian Wood (1965) and later took lessons from Ravi Shankar; The Byrds and The Rolling Stones, with Paint It Black (1966), also used the sound. Long drones and modal melodies became a hallmark of psychedelic rock.
genres.listen: Listen to Norwegian Wood and notice how the sitar follows the melody of the acoustic guitar.

genres.name: Powerpop
genres.text: Powerpop is guitar pop with the melodies and vocal harmonies of the early Beatles and the force of loud guitars. In the early 1970s Badfinger, Raspberries and Big Star played it, later followed by Cheap Trick and The Knack. In 1994 Weezer's Buddy Holly was a love letter to the 1950s, with heavily distorted guitars: powerpop for the alternative rock generation.
genres.listen: Listen to Buddy Holly and notice the cheerful pop melody above a wall of distorted guitars.

mixtapes.heading: Britpop, art rock en nu metal

genres.name: Symphonic metal
genres.text: Symphonic metal combines heavy guitars and drums with orchestral sounds, choirs and a classically trained voice. The Netherlands became a centre of the style: Within Temptation, formed in 1996 around singer Sharon den Adel, and Epica, formed in 2002, play at festivals all over the world.
genres.listen: Listen to Mother Earth and notice how the orchestra and choir rise above the distorted guitars, with the clear voice of Sharon den Adel.

genres.name: New jack swing
genres.text: In the late 1980s, in New York, producer Teddy Riley combined the vocals of R&B with the beats of hip hop: new jack swing. The drum machine swings, with a short, hard snare, while singers such as Bobby Brown and Keith Sweat sing soulfully over the top. In the early 1990s new jack swing grew into hip hop soul.
genres.listen: Listen to My Prerogative and notice the swinging drum machine and the hard snare beneath the vocals of Bobby Brown.

genres.name: Garage
genres.text: The Paradise Garage in New York, with DJ Larry Levan, was one of the most important clubs in dance music from 1977 to 1987. When disco disappeared from the charts, the music lived on there, with soulful vocals and gospel influences: garage, named after the club. In the 1990s that style gave rise to UK garage in England.
genres.listen: Listen to That's the Way Love Is and notice the soulful vocals and the piano chords over a house beat.

genres.name: Jungle and drum and bass
genres.text: In the early 1990s London producers sped up the breakbeats of rave to 160 to 180 bpm and set a deep, slow bassline beneath them, borrowed from reggae and dub: jungle. In the mid-1990s the style became tighter and more technical and took the name drum and bass, with Goldie, Roni Size and LTJ Bukem among its best-known names.
genres.listen: Listen to Inner City Life and notice the fast, broken drums set against the calm vocals and the long chords.

genres.name: Big beat
genres.text: Big beat combined the breakbeats of hip hop with rock guitars, samples and the sound of rave. The Chemical Brothers, The Prodigy and Fatboy Slim from Brighton scored big hits with it in the late 1990s, such as The Rockafeller Skank (1998).
genres.listen: Listen to The Rockafeller Skank and notice how a single sampled phrase and a guitar riff are repeated over and over above a heavy breakbeat.

genres.name: IDM
genres.text: IDM, intelligent dance music, is electronic music for listening to rather than dancing to. In 1992 the Sheffield label Warp released the compilation Artificial Intelligence, and Aphex Twin, Autechre and Boards of Canada made music with intricate rhythms, unusual sounds and ambient-like melodies.
genres.listen: Listen to Xtal and notice the soft chords and a wordless voice above a simple beat.

genres.name: Dubstep
genres.text: Dubstep emerged in the early 2000s in South London, around Croydon, out of UK garage, jungle and dub: a tempo of around 140 bpm, a rhythm with the snare on the third beat, so that it feels half as fast, and a heavy sub-bass. In America, around 2010, Skrillex made dubstep hard and loud, with a distorted wobble bass that itself becomes the melody.
genres.listen: Listen to Midnight Request Line and notice the space in the slow rhythm and the deep bass beneath it.

genres.name: Synthwave
genres.text: Synthwave is electronic music that recreates the sound of the 1980s: analogue synthesizers, reverb-drenched drums, arpeggios borrowed from Italo disco, and images of neon and old films. French producers such as Kavinsky and College made it popular in the mid-2000s; Nightcall (2010) was featured in the film Drive (2011). The Weeknd also used those sounds in Blinding Lights.
genres.listen: Listen to Nightcall and notice the slow beat, the distorted voice and the synthesizers that recall the 1980s.

genres.name: Downtempo, lounge and chill-out
genres.text: Downtempo is slow, atmospheric electronic music with a beat. In the 1990s clubs had separate chill-out rooms, and on Ibiza Café del Mar played mellow records at sunset. The softer strands of trip hop and nu jazz found their way into cafés and hotels and onto compilation albums with names like lounge or chill-out.
genres.listen: Listen to La Femme d'Argent and notice the slow groove, the electric piano and the soft synthesizers.

genres.name: K-pop
genres.text: K-pop is South Korean pop music that grew from 1992 onwards, when Seo Taiji and Boys sang hip hop and rock in Korean. Large entertainment companies train young artists for years in singing, dancing and performance and assemble them into groups, with teams of songwriters and producers from Korea and abroad. That idea of a team turning out hits at high speed had appeared earlier with Stock Aitken Waterman and Max Martin. With Dynamite (2020), BTS became the first Korean act to reach number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
genres.listen: Listen to Dynamite and notice the tight disco groove and the vocals shared out among the members of the group.

mixtapes.heading: British Eurobeat en Stock Aitken Waterman

genres.name: Schlager
genres.text: Schlager is the German word for a hit, and it became the name for melodic, sentimental popular songs in German and Dutch. In the 1950s and 1960s schlager dominated the German charts, with singers such as Freddy Quinn and later Udo Jürgens and Heino. Until the Neue Deutsche Welle, German-language pop music was mostly schlager, and in the Netherlands too, for a long time a song with Dutch lyrics quickly sounded like schlager or cabaret.
genres.listen: Listen to Griechischer Wein and notice the singalong melody, the large orchestra and the lyrics full of homesickness.

genres.name: Levenslied and smartlap
genres.text: The levenslied, literally 'song of life', is the Dutch-language song about love, sorrow, mother and the city, with a simple melody that everyone can sing along to. Its roots lie with the street singers and the smartlappen, songs full of drama. In the 1950s Amsterdam's Jordaan district became its centre, with Johnny Jordaan and Tante Leen, and in the 1980s André Hazes made the levenslied big.
genres.listen: Listen to Geef mij maar Amsterdam and notice the waltzing accompaniment and the lyrics that sing the praises of the singer's own city.

tracks.title: Ach vaderlief, toe drink niet meer

genres.name: West African music traditions
genres.text: Between the sixteenth and the nineteenth centuries more than twelve million Africans were shipped to the Americas as slaves, most of them from West and Central Africa. They brought music that was unknown in Europe: rhythms in several layers at once, call and response between a lead singer and a group, music as a fixed part of work, dance and faith, and instruments from which the banjo descended. In Congo Square in New Orleans, enslaved Africans were allowed to dance, sing and drum on Sundays until well into the nineteenth century. Those elements run through almost all the African American music that followed.
genres.listen: Listen to this field recording of Atsiagbekor, an old war dance of the Ewe people in Ghana: can you hear how the drums and the bell each play their own pattern, layered on top of each other, and how the group answers the lead singer?

genres.name: Work songs and field hollers
genres.text: On the cotton and sugar plantations of the southern United States, enslaved Africans sang while they worked. In work songs a lead singer sings a line and the group answers, in the rhythm of the work: call and response. A field holler is the calling and singing of a single person out in the fields, with a free approach to pitch. In church and at secret gatherings the spirituals came into being. After the abolition of slavery in 1865 these forms lived on, among other places in prisons and work gangs, where Alan Lomax recorded them in the twentieth century.
genres.listen: Listen to Po' Lazarus and notice the lead singer and the group answering him, with the blows of the axes as the rhythm.

genres.name: European art music
genres.text: From Europe came the harmony of art music: major and minor, chords with a fixed function, melodies in regular phrases, and music that was written down. The colonists also brought hymns, marches, dances such as the waltz and the polka, and the song for voice and piano in the parlour. In the nineteenth century sheet music and the piano made that music commonplace in America too. Ragtime owes its notation, its form and its piano to European music, and Tin Pan Alley and the spirituals sung in harmony also built on it.
genres.listen: Listen to An der schönen blauen Donau and notice the waltz in three beats and the melody moving in regular phrases.

tracks.artist: John Philip Sousa · Marine Band of the Royal Netherlands Navy
tracks.title: The Stars and Stripes Forever

genres.name: British and Irish folk music
genres.text: From the eighteenth century onwards, immigrants from Scotland, England and Ireland settled in the Appalachians. They brought ballads with them, long narrative songs about love, murder and misfortune that were passed on from singer to singer, and dance music for the fiddle, such as jigs and reels. That is how songs like Barbara Allen arrived in America. This tradition is the foundation of Appalachian folk and of country, and through the folk revival of the singer-songwriters as well.
genres.listen: Listen to Barbara Allen, an unaccompanied ballad in which each verse tells a little more of the story.

tracks.title: Tarbolton / The Longford Collector / The Sailor's Bonnet

genres.name: Minstrel shows
genres.text: From the 1830s onwards, white performers with blacked-up faces appeared in minstrel shows: blackface entertainments in which Black Americans were ridiculed, with songs, dances and sketches supposedly drawn from life on the plantation. The stock character Jim Crow later gave his name to the laws that kept Black and white people segregated. The minstrel show was also the first major form of popular entertainment in America: through these shows the banjo found its way into white music, songwriters such as Stephen Foster wrote for them, and after the Civil War Black performers appeared in them too. It is a painful origin, but one that shows how intertwined the traditions were.
genres.listen: There is deliberately no clip here. Read in the School of Rock reader how the banjo found its way into country through these shows.

tracks.title: Keep My Skillet Good and Greasy

genres.name: Krontjong
genres.text: Krontjong originated in Batavia, present-day Jakarta, from songs that Portuguese sailors brought with them from the sixteenth century onwards. Small string instruments resembling the ukulele play a rippling rhythm beneath a richly ornamented vocal line, joined by flute, violin and cello. In the 1920s and 1930s krontjong became popular throughout Indonesia through radio and film; Bengawan Solo (1940) by Gesang became a classic. After 1949 Indo-Dutch people brought the music with them to the Netherlands, where it became one of the roots of indorock.
genres.listen: Listen to Bengawan Solo and notice the rippling accompaniment of the small string instruments beneath the calm vocals.

genres.name: Indian classical music
genres.text: The classical music of North India is built on the raga, a scale with fixed melodic turns and a mood of its own, and the tala, a rhythmic cycle. A performance often begins slowly and freely, over a sustained keynote, the drone, and then speeds up together with the tabla. In the 1960s sitar player Ravi Shankar brought this music to the West: he taught George Harrison and played at the Monterey (1967) and Woodstock (1969) festivals.
genres.listen: Listen to the alap of Raga Malkauns and notice how the sitar begins freely, without a fixed metre, above the sustained drone: the raga is built up note by note.

tracks.artist: Shivkumar Sharma, Brij Bhushan Kabra & Hariprasad Chaurasia
tracks.title: Ahir Bhairav / Nat Bhairav

genres.name: Highlife
genres.text: Highlife grew up in Ghana in the first half of the twentieth century out of West African rhythms, church songs and the music of military bands and sailors. In the 1950s trumpeter E.T. Mensah, the King of Highlife, turned it into dance-band music with horns and jazz influences. Alongside this there was guitar-band highlife, with several guitars playing short, interlocking patterns. Highlife and jazz later gave rise to afrobeat in Nigeria.
genres.listen: Listen to Queen's Visit and notice the horns and the guitars playing short, repeated, interlocking patterns above a light, danceable groove.

genres.name: Afrobeat
genres.text: Around 1970, in Lagos, Fela Kuti mixed highlife with jazz and the funk of James Brown: afrobeat. With his band Africa 70 and drummer Tony Allen he played long tracks of ten minutes or more, with repeated guitar patterns, horns and a driving rhythm. In his lyrics Fela attacked Nigeria's military government, which brought him arrests and violence. Zombie (1976) is a mocking song about soldiers who follow orders without thinking.
genres.listen: Listen to Zombie and notice how the drums, bass and guitars build a long groove before the horns and the voice of Fela come in.

genres.name: Raï
genres.text: Raï comes from Oran in Algeria, where singers in cafés and at celebrations sang folk songs about love, drink and life, subjects that had no place in traditional music. In the 1980s synthesizers, drum machines and electric guitars were added: pop-raï. Singers were given the title Cheb, meaning young man; Cheb Khaled became the best known and also had a hit in Europe with Didi (1992).
genres.listen: Listen to Didi and notice the synthesizers and the drum machine beneath the Arabic vocals with their long ornaments.

genres.name: Afrobeats
genres.text: Afrobeats is the West African pop music of the 2010s: danceable tracks with a relaxed rhythm, vocals in English, Pidgin and Yoruba, and influences from dancehall, R&B and hip hop. It is something different from the afrobeat of Fela Kuti, although the name honours that forerunner. Wizkid, Davido and Burna Boy became global stars; Wizkid featured on One Dance (2016) by Drake, and Burna Boy won a Grammy in 2021.
genres.listen: Listen to Essence and notice the slow, swaying rhythm with its light percussion and the vocals lying relaxed on top.

genres.name: Calypso
genres.text: Calypso comes from Trinidad, where singers at carnival used humour and mockery to comment on politics and everyday life. From the 1930s onwards calypso was recorded and became known in America too.
