In 1948, on arriving in England aboard the ship Empire Windrush, Lord Kitchener sang London Is the Place for Me, which he recorded two years later. Calypso influenced the music of the whole Caribbean, including that of Jamaica.
genres.listen: Listen to London Is the Place for Me and notice how the singing is almost spoken, with lyrics full of detail and a swinging band beneath.

tracks.title: London Is the Place for Me

genres.name: Mento
genres.text: Mento is the folk music of rural Jamaica, played on banjo, guitar and the rumba box, a large thumb piano that provides the bass. In the 1950s mento was put on record for the first time, often with lyrics full of double meanings. Mento was sometimes called calypso, but it is a style of its own. It is one of the roots of ska.
genres.listen: Listen for the banjo, the guitar and the deep notes of the rumba box in the light, bouncing rhythm.

genres.name: Tango
genres.text: Tango originated in the late nineteenth century in the port districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, where European immigrants, Afro-Argentines and people from the countryside came together. Its rhythm has roots in the habanera, and the bandoneón, a type of concertina from Germany, became its most important instrument. The singer Carlos Gardel made tango world-famous in the 1920s and 1930s; from the 1950s onwards Astor Piazzolla renewed it with influences from jazz and classical music.
genres.listen: Listen to Por una Cabeza and notice the bandoneón and the violins, and the rhythm that keeps holding back for a moment before pushing on.

tracks.artist: Juan D'Arienzo y su Orquesta Típica
tracks.title: La Cumparsita

genres.name: Reggaeton
genres.text: Reggaeton grew up in the 1990s in Panama and Puerto Rico out of Jamaican dancehall and hip hop, sung in Spanish. Its foundation is the dembow rhythm, named after Dem Bow (1990) by Shabba Ranks: a pounding bass drum with a snare that falls just before and on the beat. Daddy Yankee scored a worldwide hit with Gasolina in 2004, and Despacito (2017) by Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee became one of the most-streamed songs ever.
genres.listen: Listen to Gasolina for the dembow rhythm: the bass drum on every beat and the snare that keeps landing just before it.

genres.name: Indopop
genres.text: Alongside the fast indorock, Indo-Dutch musicians in the Netherlands also made soft, melodic pop, with two-part vocal harmonies in the style of the Everly Brothers. The brothers Riem and Ruud de Wolff, The Blue Diamonds, had a number 1 hit in Germany and the Netherlands in 1960 with Ramona. Anneke Grönloh, born in Indonesia, scored a hit in 1962 with Brandend zand.
genres.listen: Listen to Ramona and notice the two-part vocal harmonies and the gentle guitar accompaniment.

genres.name: City pop
genres.text: City pop is the smooth, sunny Japanese pop of the late 1970s and the 1980s, made for a country that was growing rich: influences from American soft rock, funk and disco, played by tight session musicians. Tatsuro Yamashita and Mariya Takeuchi were the big names. Around 2017 Plastic Love (1984) by Takeuchi became an internet hit through YouTube, and city pop found a new, worldwide audience.
genres.listen: Listen to Plastic Love and notice the funky bassline, the horns and the cool, clear production.

genres.name: J-pop
genres.text: In the late 1980s the term J-pop came into use in Japan for modern Japanese pop music, distinct from the older, schlager-like kayōkyoku. In the 1990s producers and female singers became stars, and Hikaru Utada's album First Love (1999), with its R&B influences, became the best-selling Japanese record ever. J-pop is closely tied to anime, games and idol groups.
genres.listen: Listen to Automatic and notice how R&B rhythms and a soft voice come together with Japanese lyrics.

genres.name: Bollywood film music
genres.text: In the Hindi films made in Mumbai, known as Bollywood, songs are a fixed part of the story. The actors do not sing themselves: playback singers record the songs, and the actors mime along with their lips. Lata Mangeshkar and her sister Asha Bhosle sang thousands of film songs between them. The music blends Indian classical and folk music with Western orchestras, jazz, rock and, later, disco and electronica.
genres.listen: Listen to the high, clear voice of the playback singer soaring above an orchestra in which Indian and Western instruments play together.

tracks.title: Aaj Phir Jeene Ki Tamanna Hai

tracks.artist: A. R. Rahman, Sukhwinder Singh & Sapna Awasthi
tracks.title: Chaiyya Chaiyya

genres.name: Bhangra
genres.text: Bhangra began as a harvest dance from the Punjab, driven by the deep beats of the dhol, a large drum. In the 1980s, British Asian bands in Birmingham and London turned it into modern dance music, with synthesisers and drum machines. Panjabi MC combined bhangra with hip hop: Mundian To Bach Ke became a hit across Europe in 2002.
genres.listen: Listen to Mundian To Bach Ke and notice the dhol rhythms and the Punjabi vocals over a hip hop beat built on the bass line from Knight Rider.

genres.name: Chanson
genres.text: French chanson is song in which the lyrics take centre stage, sung with great expression, often with a small orchestra or just a piano or accordion. Édith Piaf became world-famous with La vie en rose (1947), and the Belgian Jacques Brel and Charles Aznavour wrote songs in the 1950s and 1960s that were translated all over the world. Scott Walker and David Bowie recorded songs by Brel, and Dutch kleinkunst, the Dutch tradition of literary cabaret song, also looked to chanson.
genres.listen: Listen to La vie en rose and notice how Piaf's voice carries the words, with the orchestra in the background.

genres.name: Cumbia
genres.text: Cumbia comes from the Caribbean coast of Colombia, where African drums, Indigenous flutes and Spanish song forms came together. In the 1940s and 1950s, dance orchestras turned it into popular music, with horns and accordion. After that, cumbia spread across Latin America, with its own variants in Mexico, Peru and Argentina.
genres.listen: Listen to La Pollera Colorá and notice the calm, swaying rhythm, with the scraping sound of the guacharaca and the horns.

genres.name: Congolese rumba and soukous
genres.text: In the 1940s, Cuban records of son and rumba were popular in the Congo. Musicians in Kinshasa made their own music out of them, with interlocking guitar parts and vocals in Lingala: Congolese rumba. In 1960 Le Grand Kallé wrote Indépendance Cha Cha, the song of independence, and Franco led OK Jazz for decades. In the 1980s a faster variant, soukous, became popular all over Africa and in Paris.
genres.listen: Listen to Indépendance Cha Cha and notice the Cuban rhythms, the guitars and the vocals celebrating the Congo's independence.

genres.name: Amapiano
genres.text: Amapiano emerged in the mid-2010s in the townships around Pretoria and Johannesburg, out of South African house and jazz. Its hallmark is the log drum, a deep, rubbery bass that works as a melody, beneath gentle piano chords and a slow house beat. In the 2020s amapiano went global; Tyla's Water (2023) won a Grammy.
genres.listen: Listen to Water and notice the log drum: the deep, rolling bass beneath the slow rhythm and the soft vocals.

tracks.artist: Kabza De Small & DJ Maphorisa feat. Ami Faku
tracks.title: Asibe Happy

genres.name: Surf rock
genres.text: In the early 1960s, young musicians in Southern California made surf rock: instrumental guitar music drenched in reverb, in which fast, repeated notes imitate the roar of the waves. In Misirlou (1962), Dick Dale played an old Middle Eastern melody in that style. The Beach Boys turned it into vocal music, with close harmonies; from there, Brian Wilson later developed the studio albums with which he challenged The Beatles.
genres.listen: Listen to Misirlou and notice the reverb-soaked guitar and the fast, repeated notes on a single string.

mixtapes.heading: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band

genres.name: Garage rock
genres.text: After the British Invasion, teenagers all over America started bands, rehearsed in the garage and recorded raw singles with a few chords, a screaming singer and a cheap organ. The Kingsmen had already had a hit with Louie Louie in 1963, The Sonics from Tacoma played harder than anyone, and ? and the Mysterians scored with 96 Tears (1966). The compilation Nuggets (1972) brought these records back into the spotlight, and punk built on them.
genres.listen: Listen to Psycho and notice the distorted guitar, the singer's scream and the pounding drums: punk, ten years too early.

genres.name: Hardcore punk
genres.text: Around 1980, American bands made punk shorter, faster and louder: hardcore. Black Flag from Los Angeles, and Minor Threat and Bad Brains from Washington, played songs of less than two minutes in small venues. They released their records themselves, on labels such as SST and Dischord, and organised their own tours: do it yourself. That scene later gave rise to grunge and emo.
genres.listen: Listen to Straight Edge and notice the breakneck tempo, the short song and the lyrics, which are shouted more than sung.

genres.name: Pop punk
genres.text: Pop punk combines the speed and guitars of punk with pop melodies and sing-along choruses. In 1994, Green Day from Berkeley with Dookie and The Offspring with Smash broke through to a mass audience. Around 2000, Blink-182 and many others followed, with videos full of humour on MTV.
genres.listen: Listen to Basket Case and notice the fast power chords beneath a melody you can sing along to after hearing it once.

mixtapes.heading: De jaren 90: grunge en de rest

genres.name: Indie pop and shoegaze
genres.text: From the late 1970s onwards, small British labels such as Rough Trade and Creation released guitar music outside the major record companies: indie, short for independent. In 1986 the music paper NME put together a cassette of young bands, C86, which gave its name to sweet, jangly indie pop. Around 1990 shoegaze emerged: bands such as My Bloody Valentine and Slowdive built walls of distorted, floating guitars, and on stage mostly looked down at their effects pedals, at their shoes.
genres.listen: Listen to Only Shallow and notice how the guitars merge into a single surging cloud of sound, with the vocals half hidden inside it.

genres.name: Emo
genres.text: Emo began in the mid-1980s in Washington, when bands such as Rites of Spring played hardcore with personal, emotional lyrics: emotional hardcore. In the 1990s the style became more melodic. Around 2000 emo became big, with Jimmy Eat World, Dashboard Confessional and My Chemical Romance, and with its own youth culture of black hair, skinny jeans and eyeliner.
genres.listen: Listen to The Middle and notice the bright guitars and the reassuring vocals: everything will be all right.

genres.name: Philly soul
genres.text: In Philadelphia, the songwriters and producers Kenneth Gamble and Leon Huff began making their own kind of soul in the late 1960s, and in 1971 they founded Philadelphia International Records. At Sigma Sound Studios the house band MFSB recorded lush soul, with strings, horns and a tight, danceable groove. The O'Jays scored with Love Train (1972), and MFSB's TSOP (1974) became the theme tune of the TV programme Soul Train. The Philly sound became one of the building blocks of disco.
genres.listen: Listen to Love Train and notice the strings and horns over a groove that just keeps rolling.

tracks.title: If You Don't Know Me by Now
Can't Get Enough of Your Love, Babe

genres.name: Northern soul
genres.text: In clubs in the north of England, such as the Twisted Wheel in Manchester and Wigan Casino (1973-1981), young people danced all night to fast American soul from the 1960s, often obscure singles that had sold poorly in America. DJs hunted fanatically for rare records. In 1970 the journalist Dave Godin came up with the name northern soul. Gloria Jones's Tainted Love (1964) was one of those records; Soft Cell later turned it into a synth-pop hit.
genres.listen: Listen to Tainted Love and notice the fast tempo and the handclaps that people danced to in the clubs.

tracks.title: Do I Love You (Indeed I Do)

genres.name: Berlin techno
genres.text: After the fall of the Wall in 1989, many buildings in East Berlin stood empty. That is where clubs such as Tresor (1991) appeared, in the vault of a former department store, where techno from Detroit and Berlin came together. In the 1990s the Love Parade grew into a street party with hundreds of thousands of visitors, and Berghain (2004) became one of the best-known clubs in the world. Berlin techno is often stark, dark and hypnotic, with long build-ups.
genres.listen: Listen to Sky and Sand and notice the long, slow build-up over a tight beat: the sound of a Berlin night.

genres.name: Trance
genres.text: Trance emerged around 1990 in Germany, mainly in Frankfurt and Berlin: electronic dance music with long build-ups, floating synthesiser chords and melodies that keep coming back. The Age of Love (1990) is considered one of the first tracks. DJs such as Sven Väth and Paul van Dyk made the genre big, and in the late 1990s trance became a Dutch export product.
genres.listen: Listen to For an Angel and notice the arpeggios that keep building towards the moment when the melody comes in in full.

genres.name: UK garage
genres.text: In the late 1990s, London DJs and producers turned American garage and house into a faster style of their own, with influences from jungle: UK garage, and later 2-step, with a skipping rhythm in which the kick drum does not fall on every beat. Pirate radio and clubs played it, and Craig David scored with Artful Dodger with Re-Rewind (1999). Grime and dubstep grew out of UK garage.
genres.listen: Listen to Re-Rewind and notice the bouncing 2-step rhythm, the deep bass and Craig David's smooth vocals.

tracks.title: Re-Rewind the Crowd Say Bo Selecta

genres.name: Southern hip hop and crunk
genres.text: From the late 1980s, the South of the United States also developed its own hip hop: Geto Boys in Houston, Three 6 Mafia in Memphis and OutKast in Atlanta, who made their debut in 1994. DJ Screw in Houston slowed records down to a syrupy sound, chopped and screwed. Around 2000, Lil Jon turned crunk into party music with shouted choruses and heavy 808 bass. Trap grew out of this Southern hip hop.
genres.listen: Listen to Get Low and notice the bare beat with the heavy 808, the shouted lines and the call to the crowd.

tracks.artist: Lil Jon & The East Side Boyz
tracks.title: Get Low

genres.name: Grime
genres.text: In the early 2000s, grime emerged in East London: rap in a London accent over fast, stark electronic beats of around 140 bpm, with influences from UK garage, jungle and dancehall. MCs took each other on over pirate radio. In 2003 Dizzee Rascal won the Mercury Prize with his debut Boy in da Corner, and later Skepta and Stormzy became major stars.
genres.listen: Listen to I Luv U and notice the cold, grinding synthesisers and Dizzee Rascal's fast, nervy flow.

genres.name: Drill
genres.text: Drill emerged around 2011 in Chicago: hard, dark rap about the violence in the neighbourhood, with Chief Keef as its best-known name. In London, young people made their own variant from around 2014, UK drill, with sliding 808 bass lines, a skipping rhythm and lyrics that often sparked controversy. After that, drill spread around the world, including to the Netherlands.
genres.listen: Listen to Love Sosa and notice the menacing synthesisers, the heavy 808 and the repeated, almost chanted lines.

genres.name: Minimal music
genres.text: In the 1960s, American composers made music out of short patterns that are repeated endlessly and change slowly. Terry Riley wrote In C (1964), in It's Gonna Rain (1965) Steve Reich let two tape loops drift slowly out of step, and Philip Glass worked with repeated arpeggios; he and Riley were inspired by Indian music. Minimal music became a source for ambient, techno and electronic music, and for bands such as The Velvet Underground.
genres.listen: Listen to Music for 18 Musicians and notice how short patterns are repeated again and again and change step by step.

genres.name: Industrial
genres.text: In the late 1970s, Throbbing Gristle from London made music out of noise, tape loops and electronics, released on their own label, Industrial Records: industrial. Cabaret Voltaire from Sheffield worked in the same way. From 1980, Einstürzende Neubauten from Berlin beat on sheets of metal and used power drills as instruments. In the late 1980s, Nine Inch Nails brought industrial into rock and the charts with Pretty Hate Machine (1989) and The Downward Spiral (1994).
genres.listen: Listen to Mr. Self Destruct, the opening track of The Downward Spiral, and notice the mechanical beat, the distorted sounds and Trent Reznor's voice moving from a whisper to a scream.

mixtapes.heading: TikTok en het einde van genres

genres.name: Hyperpop
genres.text: Hyperpop exaggerates everything about pop: high, distorted voices with Auto-Tune, garish synthesisers, hard bass and sudden twists. Its roots lie with A. G. Cook's London label PC Music and with the producer SOPHIE, from 2013. The name came into use in 2019 through a Spotify playlist, with 100 gecs as a well-known act, and in 2024 Charli XCX brought the style to a mass audience with Brat.
genres.listen: Listen to Immaterial and notice the metallic synthesisers, the high voices and the cheerful exaggeration.

genres.name: Barbershop
genres.text: Barbershop is singing for four men without instruments: the lead sings the melody, the tenor sings above it, and the baritone and bass fill out the chord. Around 1900 it was mainly Black Americans who sang this way, in barbershops, on the street and in church, and later jazz musicians also learned harmony from it. Its hallmark is the barbershop chord, a seventh chord that sounds so perfectly in tune that it seems to buzz. In 1904 the Haydn Quartet had a big hit in this style with Sweet Adeline.
genres.listen: Listen to Sweet Adeline and notice how four voices together form a single chord and how the long final notes hang in the air, while the other voices move around the melody.

tracks.title: It's a Long Way to Tipperary

genres.name: Fado
genres.text: Fado emerged in the first half of the nineteenth century in the poor harbour districts of Lisbon, such as Mouraria and Alfama. The word means fate. A singer, the fadista, sings of loss and longing, in Portuguese saudade, accompanied by a twelve-string Portuguese guitar and an ordinary guitar. Maria Severa became the first famous fadista around 1840. Amália Rodrigues made fado world-famous from the 1940s onwards. Since 2011 fado has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
genres.listen: Listen to Barco Negro and notice how the Portuguese guitar plays around the voice with bright, trembling notes, and how Amália Rodrigues lets the long notes swell.

genres.name: Rebetiko
genres.text: Rebetiko is the music of the Greek harbour districts, above all Piraeus near Athens. After 1922, more than a million Greek refugees came to Greece from Asia Minor, present-day Turkey, bringing their café music full of Eastern scales. In the 1930s, Markos Vamvakaris made the bouzouki, a long-necked lute, the main instrument. The songs are about poverty, love, prison and hashish. After the war, Vassilis Tsitsanis made rebetiko popular throughout Greece.
genres.listen: Listen to Frangosyriani and notice the bright, plucked bouzouki and the calm dance rhythm of the hasapiko, an old Greek dance.

genres.name: Garage rock revival
genres.text: In 2001 guitar rock suddenly sounded raw and short again. The Strokes from New York released Is This It, and The White Stripes, a duo from Detroit with just guitar and drums, released White Blood Cells. They went back to the garage rock of the 1960s and to punk: few chords, a dry recording and no long solos. More bands with 'The' in their name followed, such as The Hives from Sweden and The Vines from Australia, and then Yeah Yeah Yeahs.
genres.listen: Listen to Last Nite and notice the two guitars locking tightly together, the dry drums and the voice of Julian Casablancas, who sounds as if he is singing down an old telephone.

genres.name: Electroclash
genres.text: Around 2001, electroclash was a collision between electronic dance music and punk. DJ Larry Tee came up with the name and in October 2001 organised the Electroclash Festival in Williamsburg, a neighbourhood of Brooklyn in New York. The music borrows the cool synthesisers and drum machines of 1980s synth-pop and electro, with detached, half-spoken vocals. Fischerspooner, Peaches, Miss Kittin & The Hacker and the British band Ladytron were the best-known names. Clothes and show mattered at least as much as the music.
genres.listen: Listen to Emerge and notice the tight drum machine and the synthesiser lines that keep building, with vocals that sound cool rather than warm.

genres.name: Hardstyle
genres.text: Around 2000, hardstyle emerged in the Netherlands, out of German hard trance and Dutch hardcore. The organisation Q-dance threw parties such as Qlubtempo and Qlimax, had the name hardstyle registered in 2002 and launched the Defqon.1 festival in 2003. The foundation is a hard, distorted kick drum, at first around 140 to 150 bpm and later faster. In between comes a reverse bass: a bass note that sounds exactly between the kick drums. On top come big synthesiser melodies. Headhunterz, Showtek and Brennan Heart became the best-known names.
genres.listen: Listen to Just Begun and notice how the bass keeps falling between the hard kick drums: the reverse bass that makes hardstyle recognisable.

genres.name: Dutch house
genres.text: Around 2008, Dutch DJs such as Chuckie, Afrojack, Laidback Luke and Hardwell made their own kind of house, also called dirty Dutch, after Chuckie's parties. Dutch house has shrill, squealing synthesiser sounds, a heavy bass and Latin American rhythms in the percussion. A track builds up to a drop, the moment when the beat and the bass burst back in. Afrojack scored in 2010 with Take Over Control, and the sound became a building block of American EDM.
genres.listen: Listen to Take Over Control and notice the high, shrill synthesiser line and how everything briefly falls silent before the heavy bass kicks back in.

genres.name: Indie folk
genres.text: Around 2008, young musicians brought back acoustic folk with the approach of indie rock: recording themselves and releasing on small record labels. On their 2008 debut, Fleet Foxes from Seattle sang in close harmony like a choir. Bon Iver recorded his first album in a hunting cabin in Wisconsin, and Mumford & Sons from London made the banjo and mandolin popular at big festivals. The songs often start quietly and grow towards an exuberant ending.
genres.listen: Listen to White Winter Hymnal and notice how the voices come in with the same line one after another, like a round, while the drums grow fuller and fuller.

genres.name: Moombahton
genres.text: In late 2009, DJ Dave Nada was playing at a party thrown by his cousin in Washington. The guests wanted to hear reggaeton, so he slowed down a Dutch house track, Afrojack's remix of Moombah, from about 128 to 108 bpm. That is how moombahton was born, a name made from Moombah and reggaeton. The tempo is slow, the rhythm is reggaeton's dembow and the sounds come from Dutch house. In 2015 Major Lazer took the sound into the charts with Lean On.
genres.listen: Listen to Que Que and notice the slow, swaying dembow rhythm beneath the harsh synthesisers of Dutch house.

genres.name: Vaporwave
genres.text: Vaporwave emerged on the internet around 2010. Daniel Lopatin, as Chuck Person, slowed down snippets of 1980s pop songs and looped them endlessly. In December 2011 Ramona Xavier, as Macintosh Plus, released the album Floral Shoppe, full of slowed-down soul, lift music and advertising jingles. The name refers to vaporware: software that is announced but never appears. Vaporwave plays with the feel of old computers, shopping centres and adverts, and is half joke, half critique of consumer society.
genres.listen: Listen to Lisa Frank 420 / Modern Computing and notice how a slowed-down snippet of Diana Ross's It's Your Move keeps starting again, as if the record is stuck.

tracks.title: リサフランク420 / 現代のコンピュー

genres.name: Lo-fi hip hop
genres.text: Lo-fi hip hop is calm, instrumental hip hop to study or relax to. Lo-fi stands for low fidelity: the sound is deliberately a little muffled, with the hiss and crackle of an old record. The beats are slow and sound a bit loose, with samples of jazz piano and guitar. Major influences were the Japanese producer Nujabes and the American J Dilla. From 2017 the French YouTube channel ChilledCow, now Lofi Girl, made the genre world-famous with a livestream that runs day and night.
genres.listen: Listen to Time: The Donut of the Heart and notice how J Dilla turns a snippet of soul by The Jackson 5 into a slow, slightly dragging loop.

tracks.title: Time: The Donut of the Heart

genres.name: Latin trap
genres.text: Latin trap is trap in Spanish, from Puerto Rico. De La Ghetto and Arcángel were already rapping over trap beats around 2007, but around 2016 it became a wave, via SoundCloud and YouTube. You can hear the 808 bass and rattling hi-hats of Atlanta trap, combined with the language and sometimes the rhythm of reggaeton. Bad Bunny broke through in 2016 with Soy Peor and Anuel AA with Sola. In 2018 I Like It by Cardi B, Bad Bunny and J Balvin reached number one in America.
genres.listen: Listen to Sola and notice the slow beat with the deep 808 bass and fast hi-hats beneath the Spanish vocals.

genres.name: Baile funk
genres.text: Baile funk, known in Brazil as funk carioca, emerged in the late 1980s at the dance parties (bailes) in the favelas of Rio de Janeiro. DJs at first played American Miami bass, fast hip hop built on the drum machine. In 1989 DJ Marlboro released the album Funk Brasil, with lyrics in Portuguese. In the late 1990s came the tamborzão, a rhythm with drums from the Afro-Brazilian tradition. Cidinho & Doca sang about life in the favela, and later Anitta brought funk into Brazilian pop.
genres.listen: Listen to Rap da Felicidade and notice the pounding drum machine beneath the chorus Eu só quero é ser feliz: all I want is to be happy.

genres.name: Neo-prog
genres.text: Neo-prog emerged around 1981 in England, when progressive rock had gone out of fashion. Young bands such as Marillion, IQ, Pallas, Pendragon and Twelfth Night took early Genesis and Camel as their model, but played with the energy and sound of the 1980s: shorter songs, glossy synthesisers and a singer who played a role on stage. Marillion from Aylesbury became the biggest. The concept album Misplaced Childhood (1985) went to number 1 in England, and Kayleigh reached number two.
genres.listen: Listen to Kayleigh and notice how the guitar carries the melody with a bright, ringing sound, while Fish sings his lyrics like a letter to a lost love.

genres.name: Tropicália and MPB
genres.text: In 1967 and 1968, Tropicália was the revolt of young Brazilian musicians against their own country's clichés. Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil combined bossa nova and samba with electric guitars, psychedelia and experimental arrangers, and sang about consumerism and the military regime. At the end of 1968 they were arrested, and in 1969 they were exiled to London. Alongside this movement grew MPB, música popular brasileira: the broad current of singers such as Elis Regina, who brought together poetic lyrics and Brazilian traditions.
genres.listen: Listen to Alegria, Alegria and hear how Caetano Veloso walks with an electric guitar through a city full of newspapers, advertising and Coca-Cola.

genres.name: Nueva canción
genres.text: Nueva canción, the 'new song', emerged in the early sixties in Chile and Argentina as an alliance of folk music, poetry and protest. Violeta Parra collected old songs from the Chilean countryside and wrote Gracias a la Vida herself. Víctor Jara made the song political, and groups such as Quilapayún and Inti-Illimani brought Andean instruments like the charango and the quena onto the stage. After the coup of 1973 Jara was murdered, and many musicians went into exile.
genres.listen: Listen to Te recuerdo Amanda and hear how Víctor Jara, with nothing but a guitar, sings about a worker who goes to the factory and never comes back.

tracks.title: El Pueblo Unido Jamás Será Vencido

genres.name: Mbalax
genres.text: Mbalax is the dance music of Senegal. In the seventies, bands in Dakar mixed Cuban son with Wolof singing and the rhythms of the sabar, a high-pitched drum played with one hand and one stick. That gives the music its nervous, dancing pattern. Youssou N'Dour made mbalax world-famous in the eighties, and in 1994 he had a European hit with 7 Seconds, recorded with Neneh Cherry.
genres.listen: Listen to Immigrés and notice the sabar, which keeps shifting the rhythm, and N'Dour's high, soaring voice.

genres.name: Jùjú
genres.text: Jùjú is the popular music of the Yoruba in Nigeria. It began in Lagos in the thirties with singers who played guitar and small drums, and I.K. Dairo made it big in the fifties and sixties. In the eighties King Sunny Adé expanded jùjú into a web of talking drums, steel guitar and several guitars weaving in and out of one another. His album Synchro System (1983) was nominated for a Grammy.
genres.listen: Listen to Ja Funmi and hear how the talking drum, with its high and low tones, seems to answer the singing while the guitars weave around it.

tracks.artist: I.K. Dairo & His Blue Spots Band
tracks.title: Salome

genres.name: Death metal
genres.text: Death metal emerged in the mid-eighties, when bands in Florida pushed the speed of hardcore punk and the darkness of heavy metal to the extreme. The guitars are tuned low and played at breakneck speed, the drums play blast beats, and the singer growls instead of singing. The lyrics deal with death, horror and decay. Death from Florida, Morbid Angel and Obituary made Tampa the centre of the scene, and in the nineties Cannibal Corpse became the best-known name.
genres.listen: Listen to Zombie Ritual and hear how the guitars move in short, chopping riffs, and how the growl is more a rhythm than a melody.

genres.name: Black metal
genres.text: The name comes from Venom, who released the album Black Metal in 1982. The movement as we know it arose around 1991 in Norway, with Mayhem, Darkthrone and Emperor. The sound is deliberately raw: shrill, tremolo-picked guitars, fast drums and screamed, throaty vocals, recorded on very modest means. Part of the scene set churches on fire, and in 1993 Mayhem guitarist Euronymous was murdered by another musician from the scene.
genres.listen: Listen to Freezing Moon and notice the guitars racing along like a swarm of snow and ice, over a rhythm that keeps speeding up and slowing down.

genres.name: Post-rock
genres.text: Post-rock uses rock instruments, but not the form of the rock song. There is often no singer, and no verse and chorus: the piece grows slowly from a quiet beginning to an enormously loud ending. Talk Talk created its forerunner in the late eighties with Spirit of Eden, Slint from Louisville released Spiderland in 1991, and groups such as Tortoise, Mogwai and Godspeed You! Black Emperor turned it into a movement in the nineties. The name was coined by the critic Simon Reynolds.
genres.listen: Listen to Mogwai Fear Satan and hear how the band stays almost silent for a long while, and how the music then bursts into a wall of guitars.

genres.name: Honky-tonk
genres.text: Honky-tonk is country for the bar room. In the forties, working men in Texas, often oil workers, gathered on Saturday nights in bars so noisy that no one could hear a band. So the music grew louder: electric guitar, steel guitar and a solid beat. Ernest Tubb and Lefty Frizzell sang about drink, infidelity and loneliness, and Hank Williams gave the genre its best-known songs. Later, George Jones carried it on in the same vein.
genres.listen: Listen to Walking the Floor Over You and hear how the electric guitar plays the melody, and how Tubb tells of his heartache almost in passing.

tracks.title: If You've Got the Money, I've Got the Time

genres.name: Nashville sound
genres.text: In the late fifties, country was losing its audience to rock 'n' roll. Producers in Nashville, such as Chet Atkins and Owen Bradley, responded with a smoother sound: strings, backing choirs and a soft piano instead of fiddle and steel guitar. This allowed Patsy Cline and Jim Reeves to score hits beyond the country world as well. The sound was called the Nashville sound, and it turned the city into a music industry. Lovers of the old style felt it had lost its soul.
genres.listen: Listen to Crazy and hear how Patsy Cline sings more softly than a country star of the forties, with strings and a choir in the background.

genres.name: Outlaw country
genres.text: In the early seventies, Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson felt that the Nashville studios had too much say. They demanded to be in charge of their own records, and moved to Austin, where hippies and cowboys went to the same venues. They wore their hair long, played with their own bands and sang about rough subjects. The compilation Wanted! The Outlaws (1976) became the first country album to go platinum.
genres.listen: Listen to Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain and hear how simply Willie Nelson sings, with almost no accompaniment, and a guitar that sounds like a conversation.

tracks.title: Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain

genres.name: Mbaqanga
genres.text: Mbaqanga, the music of the township, emerged around 1960 in Johannesburg and Soweto. Black musicians combined South African folk music with American swing and jazz, creating a cheerful, swinging sound with electric bass, saxophone and choral singing. Mahlathini, the Lion of Soweto, sang in a deep, growling voice, and the Mahotella Queens sang high and close against it. In 1986 Paul Simon made the genre known around the world with Graceland, even though apartheid was still working against the music.
genres.listen: Listen to Kazet and hear how Mahlathini's deep voice is answered by the high, tight singing of the Queens, over a bouncy bass.

genres.name: Kwaito
genres.text: Kwaito is the music of South Africa's first free generation. After the end of apartheid in 1994, young people in the townships of Johannesburg created a slow, danceable sound out of house, hip-hop and local singing. The tempo is lower than in house, the bass is heavy, and the vocals often slip into talking in street slang. Boom Shaka, Bongo Maffin and Brenda Fassie became the faces of this new South Africa. The name comes from Afrikaans and means something like angry or hot.
genres.listen: Listen to It's About Time and notice the slow tempo, the heavy bass and the vocals that are half rap, half singing.

genres.name: Gqom
genres.text: Gqom is the dark, hard dance music of Durban. Around 2010, young producers in the townships made beats on cheap laptops with standard software, and shared them via mobile phones. The rhythm is bare and hard, the bass heavy, and the vocals often consist of short shouts. Babes Wodumo and Distruction Boyz took it into the charts in 2016 and 2017, and producers in London and Berlin picked up the sound. The name comes from Zulu and means roughly 'drumbeat'.
genres.listen: Listen to Wololo and hear how the beat contains hardly any melody, and how Babes Wodumo sings over it in short, exuberant shouts.

genres.name: Dangdut
genres.text: Dangdut is the popular dance music of Indonesia. The name imitates the sound of the drum, the tabla, which goes 'dang' and 'dut'. The music mixes Malay and Arabic melodies, Indian film music and rock. Rhoma Irama, the king of dangdut, gave the genre an electric guitar and a message around 1970, and Elvy Sukaesih became its queen. In 2003 Inul Daratista's hip movements sparked a nationwide debate about what counts as decent.
genres.listen: Listen to Begadang and hear how the tabla sets the rhythm, and how the electric guitar plays a melody with an Arabic colour over it.

genres.name: Mandopop and Cantopop
genres.text: Mandopop and Cantopop are pop music in Mandarin and Cantonese. Cantonese-language Cantopop arose in Hong Kong in the seventies, when Sam Hui began singing in his own language rather than in English. With her soft, clear voice, Teresa Teng from Taiwan became the greatest female singer in Mandarin, and Leslie Cheung was the star of the eighties. In the 2000s Jay Chou became the big name, with his blend of R&B, hip-hop and Chinese melodies.
genres.listen: Listen to 月亮代表我的心 and hear how Teresa Teng sings softly, almost in a whisper, with strings carrying the melody.

genres.name: Power metal
genres.text: Power metal is heavy metal that sounds fast, high and hopeful. In 1987 Helloween from Hamburg laid its foundations with Keeper of the Seven Keys: lightning-fast guitars, double bass drums and a singer who climbs into the high notes. The lyrics are about heroes, dragons and fantasy worlds. In the nineties Blind Guardian and Sonata Arctica brought the genre to a large audience, especially in Germany and Finland.
genres.listen: Listen to Future World and hear how the guitars play a cheerful melody, and how the singer delivers the chorus like a song you can roar along to.

genres.name: Metalcore
genres.text: Metalcore combines the riffs of heavy metal with the rage and the breakdowns of hardcore punk. The movement emerged in the late nineties in the north-east of the United States, with bands such as Converge from Massachusetts. The vocals switch between screaming and melodic choruses, and in the middle of a fast passage the guitars drop into a slow, leaden breakdown. In the 2000s, with Killswitch Engage and Bullet for My Valentine, metalcore became a major genre for teenagers.
genres.listen: Listen to My Last Serenade and hear how the singer leaps from screaming to singing within a single song, and how the guitars then drop into a slow breakdown.

genres.name: Dream pop
genres.text: Dream pop sounds like a dream: soft, drenched in reverb, with vocals floating above the music. In 1984 Cocteau Twins, from Grangemouth in Scotland, laid the foundations with Treasure. Guitarist Robin Guthrie built walls of echo, and singer Elizabeth Fraser sang lyrics that are almost impossible to make out, sometimes in invented words. Mazzy Star reached the charts in 1993 with Fade into You, and in the 2000s Beach House gave the style a second life.
genres.listen: Listen to Fade into You and hear how the slide guitar slowly creeps forward while Hope Sandoval sings almost in a whisper.

genres.name: Post-grunge
genres.text: Post-grunge is rock that takes over the heavy, raw guitar sound of grunge, but without the darkness, and with slickly produced choruses made for radio. After the death of Kurt Cobain in 1994, bands such as Bush from London took Nirvana's place. In the nineties and 2000s Creed and Nickelback made it the most-played rock sound in America. Critics accused the genre of turning the power of grunge into something predictable.
genres.listen: Listen to How You Remind Me and hear how the guitars sound heavy and low, while the chorus is built so that you can sing along straight away.

genres.name: Madchester
genres.text: Madchester was the dance scene of Manchester around 1989. Rock bands such as Happy Mondays and The Stone Roses combined guitar pop with the beats of acid house, and audiences went to the Hacienda instead of to rock venues. Shaun Ryder sang like a nonchalant storyteller over the Mondays' rhythm, and in 1989 The Stone Roses released a debut album that is regarded in England as one of the best ever made. The movement paved the way for Britpop.
genres.listen: Listen to Fools Gold and hear how a long, funky bassline and a dance rhythm keep going for nine minutes, while the singer sings over them almost in passing.

genres.name: Yacht rock
genres.text: Yacht rock is the smooth West Coast rock of the late seventies and early eighties. Session musicians in Los Angeles played a supple mix of pop, soul and jazz: tight rhythm sections, electric piano and vocals that sound soft and effortless. Steely Dan, The Doobie Brothers with Michael McDonald, and Christopher Cross scored big hits. The name did not exist yet at the time; it only came in 2005, from a humorous web series about this music.
genres.listen: Listen to What a Fool Believes and hear how the electric piano plays a rolling riff, after which Michael McDonald's soulful voice gently rides along.

genres.name: Blue-eyed soul
genres.text: Blue-eyed soul is soul sung by white singers. The name came in the sixties from radio DJs who played black music. In 1964 The Righteous Brothers sang You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' within the Wall of Sound of producer Phil Spector. In 1968 Dusty Springfield recorded the album Dusty in Memphis in Memphis, with the session musicians who also played for Aretha Franklin. In the seventies Daryl Hall and John Oates took the genre into the pop charts.
genres.listen: Listen to Son of a Preacher Man and hear how Dusty Springfield keeps her voice small, while the organ and the backing singers add the gospel colour.

genres.name: Quiet storm
genres.text: Quiet storm is soft, sensual soul for late at night. The name comes from Smokey Robinson's album Quiet Storm (1975). In 1976 a Howard University radio station in Washington started a late-night programme under that name: slow soul, ballads and jazzy singing, without any hurry. The format was taken up by many stations. Luther Vandross, Sade and Anita Baker became the best-known voices of the genre.
genres.listen: Listen to No Ordinary Love and hear how Sade sings almost in a whisper above a calm, low bass and slow drums.

tracks.title: A House Is Not a Home

genres.name: Go-go
genres.text: Go-go is the funk of Washington D.C., a music that never stops. Around 1975 guitarist Chuck Brown came up with a sound in which the band leaves no pause between songs and the rhythm section, with congas and lots of percussion, keeps on playing. The singer talks to the audience and the audience answers. In 1979 Bustin' Loose by Chuck Brown & the Soul Searchers topped the R&B chart. In the eighties Trouble Funk and E.U. took go-go to the whole country.
genres.listen: Listen to Bustin' Loose and hear how the percussion carries the rhythm along without a break, and how the singer and the band keep answering each other.

genres.name: Boom bap
genres.text: Boom bap is the classic hip-hop of New York in the nineties. The name imitates the rhythm: 'boom' for the bass drum, 'bap' for the snare. Producers such as DJ Premier of Gang Starr, RZA of Wu-Tang Clan and Pete Rock built their beats from short snippets of old jazz and soul, which they sampled and repeated in loops. On top of that comes the rap, with long, dense lyrics. With Illmatic (1994), Nas showed how many stories could fit into a beat like that.
genres.listen: Listen to Step in the Arena and hear how a short, dusty sample keeps coming back under a hard bass drum and a dry snare.

genres.name: Cloud rap
genres.text: Cloud rap sounds like hip-hop under water. The beats are slow, the samples full of reverb, and the vocals soft and floating, often with ambient-like textures. Around 2010 producer Clams Casino from New Jersey made beats like these for Lil B and A$AP Rocky, who broke through in 2011 with his mixtape Live.Love.A$AP. In 2013 the Swede Yung Lean took up the sound in his own melancholy version. The name came from online fans.
genres.listen: Listen to I'm God and hear how Imogen Heap's voice has been transformed into a floating, distorted choir above a slow, heavy beat.

genres.name: Goa trance and psytrance
genres.text: Goa trance emerged in the early nineties on the beaches of Goa in India, where travellers from Europe and Israel partied. The music mixed the repetition of techno with Indian melodies and many layers of synthesiser sounds. During the nineties it moved to Israel and Europe, and became faster and darker: psytrance. In Hallucinogen and Astral Projection you can hear the old sound; Infected Mushroom from Israel later made it known around the world.
genres.listen: Listen to LSD and hear how a synthesiser line runs on endlessly while new sounds keep joining in, until the track becomes a spinning pattern.

genres.name: Nu-disco
genres.text: Nu-disco brings back the dance floor of the seventies and eighties, but with modern machines. Around 2005, producers in Norway such as Lindstrøm and Todd Terje made long, unhurried tracks with analogue synthesisers and a warm bass groove. The sound earned the nickname space disco. In 2013 Daft Punk took it up in Get Lucky, with Nile Rodgers on guitar and Pharrell Williams singing, and it became a worldwide hit.
genres.listen: Listen to Get Lucky and hear how Nile Rodgers' guitar lands short and tight on the beat, while the bass and drums lay down a relaxed groove.

genres.name: Cage and Fluxus
genres.text: John Cage wondered what music still is when the composer steps back. In 4'33'' (1952) the pianist plays nothing for four minutes and thirty-three seconds, and you hear the hall. Cage used chance, dice and the Chinese I Ching to compose. His ideas found their way to the artists of Fluxus, a sixties movement around George Maciunas, in which concerts consist of everyday actions, jokes and instructions. Yoko Ono was part of it too.
genres.listen: Listen to 4'33'' and notice what you hear when no one is playing: your own breathing, the hall and the sounds from outside.

genres.name: Noise
genres.text: Noise makes music out of sheer racket: no scale, no metre, no chorus. Masami Akita started out in Tokyo in 1979 under the name Merzbow. He built walls of hissing, squealing and distortion, and named himself after the Merzbau of the Dadaist Kurt Schwitters. In England, Throbbing Gristle and Whitehouse had come first. A noise concert is often short and extremely loud, and for many listeners it is an almost physical experience rather than a musical one.
genres.listen: Listen to Woodpecker No. 1 and hear how sound without melody or metre takes on a rhythm of its own, like a machine that starts pounding faster and faster.

genres.name: Desert blues
genres.text: Desert blues, also called assouf, is the music of the Tuareg of the Sahara in Mali and Niger. Tinariwen formed in the late seventies among Tuareg exiles in Algeria and Libya, who picked up electric guitars and sang about exile and longing for the desert. The music revolves around trance-like guitar riffs, call-and-response singing and handclaps. The name blues fits because Ali Farka Touré from Mali and American blues musicians often refer to each other. In 2012 Tinariwen won a Grammy.
genres.listen: Listen to Cler Achel and hear how the guitar repeats a short riff over and over, while the singing and the handclaps of the chorus wash over it.

genres.name: Celtic folk
genres.text: Celtic folk is Irish traditional music played as a band. The Chieftains started in Dublin in 1962 with uilleann pipes, flute, fiddle and harp. In 1970 a family from Gweedore in Donegal founded Clannad, who sang old songs in Irish, with soft harmonies and later synthesisers. Their Theme from Harry's Game reached number five in England in 1982 and showed that Celtic sounds could be pop music too.
genres.listen: Listen to Theme from Harry's Game and hear how the voices, singing in Irish, float like a choir above a slow synthesiser.

genres.name: Celtic new age
genres.text: Enya was a member of Clannad from 1980 to 1982 and then went solo, with producer Nicky Ryan and lyricist Roma Ryan. In their studio in Dublin they layered her voice over and over itself, above soft synthesisers. In 1988 Orinoco Flow spent three weeks at number 1 in England, and Enya went on to win four Grammys for Best New Age Album. In this way the Celtic sound grew into a soothing style of music popular all over the world.
genres.listen: Listen to Orinoco Flow and hear how Enya's own voice is layered over itself like a choir, above a soft blanket of synthesisers.
